topics.name: Carbohydrates – Classification & Structure
topics.summary: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that yield such units on hydrolysis. They are classified into three groups based on hydrolysis behaviour: monosaccharides (cannot be hydrolysed into simpler units, e.g. glucose, fructose), oligosaccharides (yield 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, e.g. the disaccharide sucrose), and polysaccharides (yield many monosaccharide units, e.g. starch, cellulose). Carbohydrates are further described as reducing or non-reducing based on whether they possess a free anomeric carbon capable of opening into a reactive aldehyde (or tautomerizing ketone) form under basic test conditions. All monosaccharides and most oligosaccharides (except sucrose) are reducing sugars; large polysaccharides behave as essentially non-reducing because a single free end is negligible relative to the whole molecule. Some biomolecules combine carbohydrate units with other classes, such as glycoproteins (carbohydrate + protein) and carbohydrate-derived vitamins.
key_formulas: Classification by hydrolysis: monosaccharide (1 unit) → oligosaccharide (2–10 units) → polysaccharide (many units)
Reducing sugar test: free -CHO (or ketose tautomerizing to -CHO) + Tollens'/Fehling's → positive result
General carbohydrate formula (many, not all): C<sub>n</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub>
topics.worked_example: Q: Why is sucrose classified as a non-reducing sugar while maltose is classified as a reducing sugar, even though both are disaccharides? A: In sucrose, the glycosidic bond specifically links the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose to each other, leaving no free anomeric carbon on either unit. In maltose, the glycosidic bond links one glucose unit's anomeric carbon to a non-anomeric carbon of the second glucose unit, leaving that second unit's anomeric carbon free to react, making maltose reducing.
common_mistakes: Assuming every disaccharide is automatically reducing or automatically non-reducing without checking which specific carbons the glycosidic bond actually links
Assuming a ketose sugar like fructose cannot be a reducing sugar just because it lacks a free aldehyde group, without accounting for its tautomerization to an aldose form under basic test conditions
Assuming a large polysaccharide has zero free anomeric ends (rather than a negligibly small proportion of one) when explaining its practically non-reducing behaviour

topics.name: Monosaccharides – Glucose Structure & Reactions
topics.summary: Glucose, an aldohexose, is the most important monosaccharide, existing predominantly as a cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose, six-membered ring) rather than a simple open chain, in equilibrium with a small proportion of open-chain form bearing a free -CHO group. Cyclization creates a new stereocentre at C1, the anomeric carbon, giving rise to two anomers, α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose, differing only in the configuration at C1. This cyclic structure explains several classical observations: glucose's mutarotation (changing optical rotation as the two anomers interconvert), its failure to give certain aldehyde-specific reactions expected of a simple open-chain aldehyde, and the loss of reactivity toward hydroxylamine once glucose pentaacetate blocks the ring-chain equilibrium. Glucose's reactions (oxidation, reduction, acetylation, osazone formation, reaction with HCN/NH<sub>2</sub>OH) form the classical chemical evidence used to establish its structure. α- and β-glucose units polymerize differently: α-links give digestible starch/glycogen, β-links give indigestible cellulose.
key_formulas: Glucose (open chain): CH<sub>2</sub>OH-(CHOH)<sub>4</sub>-CHO (aldohexose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>)
Cyclization: C1 (aldehyde) + C5-OH → six-membered pyranose ring + new anomeric centre at C1
Glucose + NH<sub>2</sub>OH → glucose oxime (confirms free -CHO in open-chain equilibrium form)
Glucose + (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O → glucose pentaacetate (confirms 5 -OH groups)
topics.worked_example: Q: Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, even though glucose itself does. What does this show? A: Since all five -OH groups, including the one at the anomeric carbon involved in the ring-chain equilibrium, are acetylated in glucose pentaacetate, the ring can no longer open to expose a free aldehyde. This is evidence that glucose exists predominantly as a cyclic structure, not a permanently open chain.
common_mistakes: Treating glucose as a simple open-chain aldehyde throughout, rather than recognising it exists predominantly as a cyclic hemiacetal in equilibrium with a small open-chain fraction
Confusing what distinguishes α- and β-D-glucose (configuration at the anomeric carbon, C1) with a difference in molecular formula or a difference between two distinct monosaccharides

Assuming α- and β-glucose polymers behave identically toward digestive enzymes, rather than recognising that enzyme specificity for the linkage geometry explains why starch/glycogen (α) are digestible but cellulose (β) is not

topics.name: Monosaccharides – Fructose & Other Sugars
topics.summary: Fructose is a ketohexose: it contains a ketone group at C2 rather than an aldehyde at C1, distinguishing it structurally from aldose sugars like glucose. Despite lacking a free aldehyde group, fructose is still classified as a reducing sugar, because under the basic conditions used in tests like Fehling's or Tollens', it can tautomerize through an enediol intermediate into isomeric aldose forms bearing a reactive -CHO group. Fructose also cyclizes, typically forming a five-membered furanose ring, and shows its own characteristic anomeric behaviour. Seliwanoff's test exploits the differing rate of acid-catalysed dehydration between ketoses and aldoses to specifically distinguish fructose from glucose. Fructose is a key component of sucrose (paired with glucose) and of some storage polysaccharides in certain plants, such as inulin, contrasting with glucose-based starch.
key_formulas: Fructose (open chain): CH<sub>2</sub>OH-CO-(CHOH)<sub>3</sub>-CH<sub>2</sub>OH (ketohexose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>)
Basic conditions: ketose ↔ enediol intermediate ↔ aldose (tautomerization enabling a positive reducing-sugar test)
Seliwanoff's test: ketose (fructose) dehydrates rapidly under hot acid → positive; aldose (glucose) → negative or much slower
topics.worked_example: Q: Fructose gives a positive Fehling's test despite having no free -CHO group in its stable form. Explain. A: Fehling's solution is basic. Under these basic conditions, fructose tautomerizes via an enediol intermediate into aldose isomers that do carry a free -CHO group; this aldehyde is what actually reduces the Cu<sup>2+</sup> in Fehling's reagent, allowing fructose to test positive as a reducing sugar.
common_mistakes: Concluding that fructose cannot be a reducing sugar simply because it is a ketone rather than an aldehyde, without considering tautomerization under basic test conditions
Confusing Seliwanoff's test (ketose-specific dehydration) with a generic carbohydrate test that would give the same result for both glucose and fructose

Assuming every fructose-containing or fructose-based polysaccharide must also contain glucose in equal proportion, rather than recognising some plant storage polysaccharides (e.g. inulin) are built predominantly from fructose alone

topics.name: Disaccharides
topics.summary: Disaccharides form when two monosaccharide units are joined by a glycosidic bond, a condensation linkage created with the loss of one water molecule. Maltose (two α-glucose units) and lactose (galactose + glucose) are reducing sugars, because their glycosidic bond leaves one unit's anomeric carbon free to react. Sucrose (glucose + fructose) is the key exception: its glycosidic bond specifically links the anomeric carbons of both monosaccharide units to each other, leaving neither free, so sucrose is non-reducing. Hydrolysing sucrose (acid or the enzyme invertase) yields an equimolar glucose-fructose mixture called invert sugar; because fructose's strong levorotation outweighs glucose's weaker dextrorotation, the net optical rotation flips from dextrorotatory (sucrose) to levorotatory (invert sugar) on hydrolysis. Enzymes that hydrolyse disaccharides (sucrase, maltase, lactase) are each specific to their own particular glycosidic linkage.
key_formulas: Glucose + Fructose → Sucrose + H<sub>2</sub>O (glycosidic bond between both anomeric carbons, C1 of glucose ↔ C2 of fructose)
2 α-Glucose → Maltose + H<sub>2</sub>O (one anomeric carbon left free → reducing)
Sucrose + H<sub>2</sub>O →(acid/invertase) Glucose + Fructose (invert sugar; optical rotation inverts, dextro → levo)
topics.worked_example: Q: Why does hydrolysing sucrose reverse the sign of optical rotation? A: Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory. Hydrolysis releases free glucose (weakly dextrorotatory) and free fructose (strongly levorotatory) in equal amounts. Since fructose's levorotation is stronger in magnitude than glucose's dextrorotation, the resulting mixture's net rotation is levorotatory overall — an 'inversion' of sign relative to sucrose, hence the name invert sugar.
common_mistakes: Assuming sucrose is non-reducing simply because it is a disaccharide in general, rather than because its specific glycosidic bond ties up both anomeric carbons

Assuming an enzyme that hydrolyses one disaccharide (e.g. sucrase acting on sucrose) will also hydrolyse a different disaccharide (e.g. maltose or lactose) with a differently configured glycosidic bond
Forgetting that 'invert sugar' refers to the reversal of optical rotation sign upon hydrolysis, not to any structural inversion or enantiomer formation in the glucose/fructose molecules themselves

topics.name: Polysaccharides
topics.summary: Polysaccharides are macromolecules built from many monosaccharide units joined by glycosidic bonds, generally not sweet and essentially non-reducing due to the negligible proportion of free ends relative to molecular size. Starch (amylose + amylopectin) and glycogen are glucose-based storage polysaccharides built via α-glycosidic linkages, readily hydrolysed by amylase (which recognises this α-linkage geometry) into maltose and ultimately glucose. Cellulose, also glucose-based but built via β-glycosidic linkages, forms rigid plant cell walls through extensive hydrogen bonding between parallel linear chains; because human digestive enzymes like amylase are specific to α-linkages, cellulose passes through the human gut largely undigested. Other polysaccharides use different monosaccharides as their building block, such as inulin (fructose-based, found in some plant roots). Polysaccharides thus illustrate how enzyme specificity for glycosidic-linkage geometry, not just choice of monosaccharide, governs digestibility and biological role.
key_formulas: Starch/glycogen: (α-D-glucose)<sub>n</sub>, α-1,4- (and, in amylopectin/glycogen, α-1,6-) glycosidic linkages
Cellulose: (β-D-glucose)<sub>n</sub>, β-1,4-glycosidic linkages
Amylase + starch (α-linkages) → maltose → glucose; amylase + cellulose (β-linkages) → no significant reaction
topics.worked_example: Q: Starch and cellulose are both glucose polymers, yet only starch is digestible by humans. Why? A: Starch's glucose units are joined by α-glycosidic linkages, which amylase's active site is shaped to recognise and hydrolyse. Cellulose's glucose units are joined by differently configured β-glycosidic linkages, which do not fit amylase's active site, so cellulose resists hydrolysis by human digestive enzymes despite using the identical monosaccharide.
common_mistakes: Assuming starch and cellulose must be built from different monosaccharides because they behave so differently, rather than recognising both use glucose and differ only in linkage geometry (α vs β)
Treating 'non-reducing' as meaning a polysaccharide has literally zero free anomeric ends, rather than a negligibly small proportion of one relative to its size
Assuming every enzyme that hydrolyses one glycosidic-linked polysaccharide will hydrolyse any other, without accounting for linkage-geometry specificity

topics.name: Amino Acids
topics.summary: Amino acids are the monomer units of proteins, each built from an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a distinguishing side-chain (R group) attached to a central (α) carbon. In solution, a free amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion, carrying both a positively charged -NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group and a negatively charged -COO<sup>-</sup> group simultaneously. Amino acids are classified as essential (the body cannot synthesise them in sufficient quantity and must obtain them from the diet) or non-essential. The ninhydrin test detects the free α-amino group characteristic of amino acids, giving a purple/blue colour. Amino acids also serve as precursors for amino-acid-derivative hormones (built by modifying a single amino acid, e.g. tyrosine into adrenaline or thyroxine) and participate in transamination reactions assisted by vitamin B6-derived coenzymes.
key_formulas: General amino acid structure: H<sub>2</sub>N-CH(R)-COOH ↔ zwitterion <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>N-CH(R)-COO<sup>-</sup>
Ninhydrin test: free α-amino group + ninhydrin → purple/blue colour
Essential amino acid: not synthesised in adequate quantity by the body → required from diet (parallel to vitamins)
topics.worked_example: Q: Why does a free amino acid carry both a positive and a negative charge (zwitterion) in solution? A: The amino group (-NH<sub>2</sub>) can accept a proton to become -NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, while the carboxyl group (-COOH) can donate a proton to become -COO<sup>-</sup>; both proton transfers occur simultaneously within the same free molecule, giving it an overall net charge of zero despite carrying both a positive and a negative site.
common_mistakes: Assuming an amino acid residue in the interior of a protein chain retains the same free -NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>/-COO<sup>-</sup> groups as a free amino acid, forgetting that peptide-bond formation on both sides consumes these groups
Confusing 'amino-acid-derivative hormone' (built by modifying a single amino acid, e.g. thyroxine) with 'peptide hormone' (built from a chain of many amino acids, e.g. insulin)
Treating the essential/non-essential amino acid classification as unrelated to the similar 'must come from diet' logic that defines a vitamin

topics.name: Proteins – Structure & Peptide Bond
topics.summary: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, a condensation linkage formed between one amino acid's carboxyl group and the next amino acid's amino group, releasing water. Only chain-terminal residues retain a free amino or carboxyl group; internal residues use both in forming peptide bonds to their neighbours. A protein's function depends not just on its amino acid sequence (primary structure) but on its correctly folded three-dimensional shape; denaturation (extreme heat or pH) disrupts this shape and destroys function (e.g. an enzyme's catalytic activity) even though the sequence itself is unchanged. The Biuret test (violet colour) and the Xanthoproteic test (yellow colour, aromatic residues) specifically detect proteins. Proteins include structural types (e.g. keratin, packed via extensive H-bonding, paralleling cellulose's structural role) and functional types (enzymes, and peptide hormones such as insulin, which is a direct translation product of its gene, unlike a steroid hormone).
key_formulas: Amino acid<sub>1</sub>-COOH + H<sub>2</sub>N-Amino acid<sub>2</sub> → peptide bond (-CO-NH-) + H<sub>2</sub>O
Biuret test: peptide bond + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (basic) → violet colour
Xanthoproteic test: aromatic amino acid residues + conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → yellow colour
topics.worked_example: Q: An enzyme loses catalytic activity on heating, even though its amino acid sequence is unchanged. Explain. A: Catalytic activity depends on the enzyme's correctly folded three-dimensional shape (its active site geometry), not on sequence alone. Heat denatures the protein by disrupting this folded shape (without breaking the peptide bonds that define the sequence), so the active site's precise arrangement is lost and catalytic activity is abolished.
common_mistakes: Assuming an internal amino acid residue within a protein chain still carries a free amino and carboxyl group, rather than recognising both are consumed in forming peptide bonds to its two neighbours
Confusing denaturation (loss of 3-D folded structure, sequence unchanged) with a change to the amino acid sequence itself

Assuming a peptide hormone like insulin and a steroid hormone would behave identically toward a peptide-bond-specific test (e.g. Biuret), rather than recognising only the peptide hormone contains peptide bonds

topics.name: Enzymes
topics.summary: Enzymes are globular proteins that catalyse specific biochemical reactions, typically showing high substrate specificity: an enzyme's active site, formed by the precise 3-D arrangement of particular amino acid side chains, is shaped to fit one substrate (or a narrow group of closely related substrates). This specificity can be sensitive even to a single stereochemical difference, as when glucose oxidase acts on β-D-glucose but not α-D-glucose, or to linkage geometry, as when amylase hydrolyses starch's α-glycosidic bonds but not cellulose's β-glycosidic bonds. Denaturation (extreme heat/pH) disrupts the folded 3-D structure and abolishes catalytic activity without altering the sequence. Many enzymes additionally require a non-protein coenzyme, often derived from a vitamin (e.g. niacin → NAD<sup>+</sup>, riboflavin → FAD), to function; without adequate coenzyme supply, the enzyme's protein portion alone cannot catalyse effectively. Enzymes such as DNA polymerase also catalyse nucleic-acid processes like replication.
key_formulas: Enzyme + Substrate → Enzyme-Substrate complex → Enzyme + Product (active-site/lock-key specificity)
Niacin (vitamin B3) → NAD<sup>+</sup> (coenzyme); Riboflavin (vitamin B2) → FAD (coenzyme)
Denaturation: correctly folded (active) enzyme →(heat/extreme pH) unfolded (inactive) enzyme, sequence unchanged
topics.worked_example: Q: Glucose oxidase acts efficiently on β-D-glucose but poorly on α-D-glucose. What does this show about enzyme specificity? A: α- and β-D-glucose are anomers, identical in molecular formula and differing only in configuration at the anomeric carbon. Glucose oxidase's active site is shaped to specifically recognise the β-configuration, so even this single stereochemical difference is enough to strongly affect binding and catalysis — enzyme specificity can be extremely fine-grained.
common_mistakes: Assuming an enzyme that acts on one substrate will act equally well on a closely related substrate (a different anomer, or a different glycosidic linkage), ignoring active-site geometry specificity
Assuming a fully intact, correctly folded enzyme protein is always sufficient for catalysis, forgetting some enzymes strictly require a non-protein coenzyme (often vitamin-derived) to function

Confusing an enzyme's role as catalyst (e.g. DNA polymerase catalysing replication) with the identity of the molecule it acts upon (DNA, a nucleic acid) — the enzyme itself remains a protein regardless of its substrate

topics.name: Vitamins
topics.summary: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal body function, which the body cannot synthesise in adequate quantity and must obtain from the diet — a dietary-essential-nutrient concept paralleling essential amino acids. Vitamins are classified as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K; often lipid/isoprenoid or cholesterol-related in structure, stored in body fat) or water-soluble (B-complex, C; generally excreted rather than stored, requiring more regular intake). Several water-soluble vitamins are precursors of essential coenzymes: niacin (B3) → NAD<sup>+</sup>, riboflavin (B2) → FAD (whose structure includes an adenine-nucleotide portion), and pyridoxine (B6) → a coenzyme assisting amino acid transamination. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is structurally and biosynthetically related to glucose, distinguishing it from vitamins with a purely lipid-related origin. Deficiency of a vitamin required for a coenzyme directly impairs the many enzymes that depend on that coenzyme, even when the enzyme's own protein portion is fully intact.
key_formulas: Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K (lipid-related structure, stored in body fat)
Water-soluble vitamins: B-complex, C (generally not stored, needed more regularly)
Vitamin → coenzyme: Niacin (B3) → NAD<sup>+</sup>; Riboflavin (B2) → FAD; Pyridoxine (B6) → transamination coenzyme
topics.worked_example: Q: A severe niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency impairs many enzymes that require NAD<sup>+</sup>, even though those enzymes' protein portions are fully intact. Explain. A: NAD<sup>+</sup> is a coenzyme derived from niacin. These enzymes require NAD<sup>+</sup> bound alongside their protein portion to catalyse their reactions. Without adequate niacin, the cell cannot produce enough NAD<sup>+</sup>, so the enzymes cannot function effectively even though nothing is wrong with their own protein structure.
common_mistakes: Treating all vitamins as chemically similar, rather than recognising the fat-soluble/water-soluble distinction reflects a genuine underlying structural difference (lipid-related vs not) with real solubility and storage consequences
Overlooking that a vitamin-derived coenzyme's deficiency impairs enzyme function even when the enzyme's protein portion itself is completely normal
Assuming vitamin C's carbohydrate-related structural origin (from glucose) applies to vitamins generally, rather than being a specific feature of vitamin C in particular

topics.name: Nucleic Acids – Nucleotide & DNA/RNA Structure
topics.summary: A nucleotide, the monomer unit of a nucleic acid, is a three-part composite: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. DNA's sugar is deoxyribose; RNA's is ribose. Because these are pentoses (5 carbons), their cyclic form is a five-membered furanose ring, in contrast to glucose (a hexose), which forms a six-membered pyranose ring. Successive nucleotides are joined into a nucleic acid's backbone by phosphodiester bonds, which alternate sugar and phosphate groups — a different linkage chemistry from a polysaccharide's direct sugar-to-sugar glycosidic-bonded backbone, though both are condensation polymers releasing water. In DNA's double helix, specific hydrogen-bonded base-pairing (adenine–thymine, guanine–cytosine; Chargaff's rule: %A = %T, %G = %C) holds the two strands together and underlies accurate semi-conservative replication. This nucleotide-based structural motif also appears in coenzymes such as FAD and NAD<sup>+</sup>, which incorporate an adenine-nucleotide portion.
key_formulas: Nucleotide = Nitrogenous base + Pentose sugar + Phosphate group
Chargaff's rule: %Adenine = %Thymine, %Guanine = %Cytosine (each G-C pair contributes exactly 1 guanine + 1 cytosine)
Nucleic acid backbone: …-sugar-phosphate-sugar-phosphate-… via phosphodiester bonds
topics.worked_example: Q: A DNA segment has 1000 total base pairs; 300 are A-T pairs. How many guanine molecules are present across both strands? A: Remaining base pairs = 1000 − 300 = 700, all G-C pairs. Since each G-C pair contributes exactly one guanine (paired with one cytosine on the complementary strand), the total number of guanine molecules is 700.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pentose sugar's furanose ring (5-membered, in nucleotides) with glucose's pyranose ring (6-membered), or assuming ring size is unrelated to the number of carbons in the sugar
In a Chargaff's-rule calculation, forgetting that each G-C base pair contributes exactly one guanine (not two), leading to answers that are doubled or halved incorrectly

Assuming a nucleic acid's phosphodiester-linked backbone and a polysaccharide's glycosidic-linked backbone are chemically identical simply because both are condensation polymers of a sugar-containing unit

topics.name: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
topics.summary: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each of the two new daughter DNA molecules contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand, a prediction directly enabled by DNA's specific base-pairing rules, which allow each original strand to serve as an unambiguous template. The genetic code, read in consecutive non-overlapping triplet codons, is degenerate (several codons can specify the same amino acid), so a point mutation that switches between two codons for the identical amino acid produces a silent mutation with no change to the protein. By contrast, a frameshift mutation (insertion/deletion of one base) shifts the entire downstream reading frame, typically disrupting most or all amino acids from that point onward — far more broadly damaging than a point mutation confined to one codon. A mutation within a gene coding for an enzyme can alter a critical active-site amino acid, impairing catalytic function; genes generally direct protein synthesis via transcription and translation, the pathway through which DNA sequence changes can affect protein structure.
key_formulas: Semi-conservative replication: 1 parental DNA duplex → 2 daughter duplexes, each = 1 old strand + 1 new strand
Genetic code: triplet codon (3 bases) → 1 amino acid; degenerate (multiple codons per amino acid possible)
Point mutation (substitution) → affects ≤1 codon; Frameshift mutation (insertion/deletion) → shifts entire downstream reading frame
topics.worked_example: Q: Why is a frameshift mutation typically far more disruptive to a protein's sequence than a point mutation? A: The genetic code is read in consecutive triplets. A point substitution changes at most the one codon containing the altered base. An insertion or deletion, however, shifts how every subsequent base is grouped into codons, scrambling most or all amino acids downstream of that point — a much larger-scale disruption than a single-codon change.
common_mistakes: Assuming any DNA base change must always alter the resulting protein, ignoring that codon degeneracy can make certain substitutions silent
Assuming a point mutation and a frameshift mutation have comparable impact simply because both start from a change at a single base position

Proposing a 'conservative' replication model's predicted outcome (both original strands staying together) as if it matched the actual semi-conservative model, rather than recognising these predict different, distinguishable strand compositions after one round of replication

topics.name: Hormones
topics.summary: Hormones are chemical messengers classified by their structural origin into three main types: peptide hormones (built from a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, e.g. insulin — a direct translation product of its gene, digestible and denatured like any protein, detectable by the Biuret test), steroid hormones (built from a cholesterol-derived framework, e.g. estrogen, testosterone, cortisol — lipid-related, structurally similar to fat-soluble vitamins, and typically synthesised via a multi-step enzymatic pathway coded for indirectly by genes rather than being a direct translation product), and amino-acid-derivative hormones (built by chemically modifying a single amino acid, e.g. tyrosine into adrenaline or thyroxine, distinct from a peptide hormone's multi-amino-acid chain). A peptide hormone taken orally is broken down by digestive enzymes before absorption (hence given by injection), while a steroid hormone's lipid-related structure lets it cross cell membranes more readily. Some hormones are glycoproteins, combining a protein/peptide backbone with an attached carbohydrate (oligosaccharide) chain.
key_formulas: Peptide hormone (e.g. insulin): amino acid chain, peptide bonds, direct gene/translation product, Biuret-positive
Steroid hormone (e.g. cortisol, estrogen): cholesterol-derived framework, genes code for its biosynthetic enzymes (not the hormone directly), lipid-soluble
Amino-acid-derivative hormone (e.g. adrenaline, thyroxine): single modified amino acid (tyrosine-derived), not a peptide chain
topics.worked_example: Q: A peptide hormone works when injected but not when taken orally, even at a much higher dose. Explain. A: As a peptide, the hormone is built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; digestive enzymes in the gut, adapted to hydrolyse peptide bonds during normal protein digestion, break it down into inactive fragments before it can be absorbed intact. Injection bypasses the digestive tract entirely, avoiding this breakdown.
common_mistakes: Confusing a peptide hormone (multi-amino-acid chain, e.g. insulin) with an amino-acid-derivative hormone (single modified amino acid, e.g. thyroxine or adrenaline) — both trace back to amino acids but have very different structures
Assuming all hormones would react identically to a protein-specific test (e.g. Biuret), rather than recognising only peptide hormones contain peptide bonds while steroid hormones do not
Assuming genes code directly for a steroid hormone's structure the same way they code for a peptide hormone, rather than recognising genes code only for the steroid's biosynthetic-pathway enzymes

questions.question: Carbohydrates are chemically defined as:
options: Esters of long-chain fatty acids with glycerol
Optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that yield such species on hydrolysis
Compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio C<sub>n</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub>
Polymers of amino acids linked through peptide bonds
questions.explanation: NCERT defines carbohydrates as optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes/ketones, or substances that hydrolyse to give such units; the older C<sub>n</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub> formula is not used as the defining criterion.
questions.hint: Think in terms of the functional group present, not just the elemental ratio.
distractor_logic: This describes fats and oils (lipids), not carbohydrates.
This is the older, now-abandoned 'hydrate of carbon' formula, which fails for sugars such as rhamnose and does not capture the defining functional group.
This describes proteins, not carbohydrates.

questions.question: On hydrolysis, sucrose yields two monosaccharide units. It is therefore classified as a:
options: Amino acid
Disaccharide
Monosaccharide
Polysaccharide
questions.explanation: A carbohydrate that yields exactly two monosaccharide units on hydrolysis is classified as a disaccharide, a type of oligosaccharide.
questions.hint: Count how many monosaccharide units are released on hydrolysis.
distractor_logic: Amino acids are the monomer units of proteins and are unrelated to the hydrolysis products of carbohydrates.
Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further into simpler units at all, so a sugar that splits into two units on hydrolysis cannot itself be one.
Polysaccharides yield a very large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, not just two.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reducing sugar from a non-reducing sugar?
options: A reducing sugar turns blue litmus red
A reducing sugar is always a polysaccharide, while a non-reducing sugar is always a monosaccharide
A reducing sugar has a free anomeric -OH group that can open to expose an aldehyde or ketone group capable of reducing Fehling's or Tollens' reagent
A reducing sugar contains more oxygen atoms per molecule than a non-reducing sugar
questions.explanation: A sugar is reducing if it has a free anomeric hydroxyl group that can open into a reactive carbonyl form, allowing it to reduce Fehling's and Tollens' reagents; sucrose lacks such a group and is non-reducing.
questions.hint: Focus on whether an anomeric -OH group is free or tied up in a glycosidic bond.
distractor_logic: This confuses the reducing-sugar test (Fehling's/Tollens') with an acid-base indicator test, which is irrelevant to a sugar's reducing property.
This reverses key facts: all monosaccharides are reducing sugars, and the classic non-reducing example, sucrose, is a disaccharide, not a polysaccharide.
Reducing character depends on whether a free anomeric group is available, not on the total oxygen content of the molecule.

questions.question: Glucose is also known by which common name?
options: Sucrose
Dextrose
Fructose
Galactose
questions.explanation: Glucose is widely known as dextrose, a name reflecting its dextrorotatory nature in aqueous solution.
questions.hint: The alternate name reflects the sugar's optical rotation.
distractor_logic: Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, not a synonym for glucose alone.
Fructose is a different ketohexose, not another name for glucose.
Galactose is a distinct aldohexose found in lactose, not an alternate name for glucose.

questions.question: On complete acetylation, glucose forms a pentaacetate. What does this observation confirm about its open-chain structure?
options: Glucose contains five carbon atoms
Glucose contains an aldehyde and a ketone group
Glucose contains five -OH groups
Glucose is a five-membered ring compound
questions.explanation: Pentaacetate formation is cited in NCERT as evidence that the open-chain structure of glucose carries five hydroxyl groups.
questions.hint: Count how many acetate groups get attached during acetylation.
distractor_logic: Glucose is a hexose with six carbon atoms; the number of acetate groups reflects hydroxyl groups, not total carbon count.
Glucose has only one carbonyl group, an aldehyde; acetylation counts -OH groups, not carbonyl groups.
Pentaacetate formation is evidence from the open-chain form about the number of -OH groups, and is unrelated to ring size.

questions.question: Which laboratory observation was historically used as evidence that glucose contains a free -CHO group in its open-chain form?
options: It does not undergo mutarotation
It reacts with sodium hydroxide to give a colourless solution
It forms an oxime with hydroxylamine, and on mild oxidation with bromine water gives a six-carbon acid (gluconic acid)
It fails the 2,4-DNP test
questions.explanation: Oxime formation with hydroxylamine and oxidation to a six-carbon acid on mild oxidation are standard evidences for a free aldehyde group in glucose's open-chain structure.
questions.hint: Recall which tests from the derivative-formation and oxidation set point specifically to -CHO.
distractor_logic: Glucose does undergo mutarotation; this phenomenon is evidence for the cyclic hemiacetal form, not the open-chain -CHO group.
This is not one of the diagnostic tests used to identify the carbonyl group of glucose.
This observation actually goes against a simple free-carbonyl open-chain picture, and is used as evidence for the cyclic structure, not for the presence of -CHO.

questions.question: In the cyclic (Haworth) structure of glucose, the six-membered pyranose ring is formed by the reaction between:
options: The -CHO group at C1 and the -OH group at C6
The -OH groups at C2 and C6
The -CHO group at C1 and the -OH group at C5
The -CHO group at C1 and the -OH group at C4
questions.explanation: The hemiacetal ring in glucose's pyranose form arises between the aldehyde carbon (C1) and the hydroxyl group on C5, giving a six-membered ring.
questions.hint: Count the ring atoms needed to form a six-membered ring starting from C1.
distractor_logic: Reaction of C1 with the C6-OH would give a seven-membered ring; glucose's pyranose ring specifically involves C5.
Ring closure in glucose involves the carbonyl carbon, C1, not two hydroxyl-bearing carbons unconnected to the carbonyl.
A C1-C4 hemiacetal linkage would give a five-membered furanose ring, not the six-membered pyranose ring glucose actually forms.

questions.question: Fructose differs from glucose in the position and nature of its carbonyl group. Fructose is best described as a:
options: Aldopentose
Ketopentose
Aldohexose
Ketohexose
questions.explanation: Fructose carries a ketonic carbonyl group at C2 of a six-carbon chain, making it a ketohexose, in contrast to glucose's aldehyde group at C1.
questions.hint: Identify the type of carbonyl group present and count the total carbon atoms.
distractor_logic: Fructose has six carbons, not five, and its carbonyl is a ketone, not an aldehyde.
Fructose is a six-carbon sugar, not a five-carbon one.
This describes glucose; fructose's defining carbonyl is a ketone, not an aldehyde.

questions.question: The cyclic structure of fructose is a five-membered ring formed by reaction of the C2 keto group with the -OH at which carbon?
options: C4
C6
C5
C1
questions.explanation: Fructose's furanose (five-membered) ring arises from hemiketal formation between the C2 carbonyl and the C5 hydroxyl group.
questions.hint: Furanose rings are five-membered; count carbons from C2 to the hydroxyl-bearing carbon involved.
distractor_logic: This would give a four-membered ring, not the furanose ring fructose actually adopts.
Reaction with the C6-OH would give a six-membered ring, but fructose's characteristic cyclic form is the five-membered furanose ring.
C1 in fructose is a -CH<sub>2</sub>OH group with no carbonyl; ring closure occurs through the C2 keto group, not through C1.

questions.question: Despite having a ketonic group, fructose still reduces Fehling's and Tollens' reagents. Which property of fructose explains this reducing behaviour?
options: Under the basic conditions of these reagents, fructose undergoes enolisation to give an aldehyde-containing tautomer
Fructose is secretly an aldohexose and its usual ketonic formula is incorrect
Fructose contains a hidden second aldehyde group at C6
Fehling's and Tollens' reagents react with any six-carbon sugar regardless of functional group
questions.explanation: Under the alkaline conditions of Fehling's and Tollens' tests, an alpha-hydroxy ketone like fructose isomerises through an enediol intermediate to an oxidisable aldehyde form, so it still tests positive as a reducing sugar.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to a ketone adjacent to an -OH group under basic conditions.
distractor_logic: Fructose genuinely is a ketohexose; its structural formula is not in error.
C6 in fructose is a primary alcohol group (-CH<sub>2</sub>OH), not an aldehyde.
Reducing tests are specific to the presence of an oxidisable free carbonyl accessible via a free anomeric centre, not simply to carbon count.

questions.question: Maltose is formed from the condensation of which two units, and with what type of glycosidic linkage?
options: β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose joined by a β-1,4-glycosidic linkage
α-D-glucose and β-D-fructose joined by a 1,2-glycosidic linkage
Two units of β-D-glucose joined by a β-1,4-glycosidic linkage
Two units of α-D-glucose joined by an α-1,4-glycosidic linkage
questions.explanation: Maltose is built from two α-D-glucose units connected through an α-1,4-glycosidic bond, leaving one free anomeric -OH group.
questions.hint: Both units in maltose are the same monosaccharide, linked in the alpha configuration.
distractor_logic: This describes lactose, not maltose.
This describes sucrose, not maltose.
β-1,4-linked glucose units describe the cellulose-type linkage, not maltose, which uses α-glucose units.

questions.question: Lactose, the sugar found in milk, is composed of which two monosaccharide units?
options: Fructose and galactose
Glucose and galactose
Two units of galactose
Glucose and fructose
questions.explanation: Lactose is a β-1,4-linked disaccharide of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose.
questions.hint: One of the two units shares its name with the sugar found in milk.
distractor_logic: This is not the composition of any of the common disaccharides in this chapter; lactose specifically pairs galactose with glucose.
Lactose contains one galactose and one glucose unit, not two identical galactose units.
This pairing describes sucrose, not lactose.

questions.question: Why is sucrose classified as a non-reducing sugar?
options: Both anomeric carbons, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, are involved in the glycosidic linkage, leaving no free anomeric -OH group
Sucrose reacts too slowly with Fehling's reagent to observe a colour change even though it has a free anomeric carbon
Sucrose is a monosaccharide, and monosaccharides never reduce Fehling's solution
Sucrose does not contain any -OH groups at all
questions.explanation: In sucrose, the glycosidic bond forms between the anomeric carbons of both glucose (C1) and fructose (C2), so neither ring can open to expose a free carbonyl, making sucrose non-reducing.
questions.hint: Compare how many anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond in sucrose versus in maltose or lactose.
distractor_logic: The correct explanation is structural: no free anomeric -OH is available at all, not a matter of slow reaction kinetics.
Sucrose is a disaccharide, and in fact all monosaccharides do reduce Fehling's solution; this statement reverses both facts.
Sucrose retains many free hydroxyl groups; what it specifically lacks is a free anomeric hydroxyl.

questions.question: Starch is composed of two structurally different fractions. What are they?
options: Cellulose and glycogen
Amylose (unbranched) and amylopectin (branched)
Maltose and sucrose
α-glucose and β-glucose in equal proportion
questions.explanation: Starch consists of the water-soluble, unbranched amylose (α-1,4 linkages) and the branched, insoluble amylopectin (α-1,4 linkages with α-1,6 branch points).
questions.hint: One fraction is a straight chain; the other has branch points.
distractor_logic: Cellulose and glycogen are entirely separate polysaccharides, not components of starch.
Maltose and sucrose are disaccharides, not the polysaccharide fractions making up starch.
Starch is built almost entirely from α-D-glucose units; the two-fraction distinction concerns chain branching, not anomeric form.

questions.question: Cellulose, unlike starch, is not digestible by humans because it is a polymer of:
options: β-D-glucose joined by β-1,4-linkages
α-D-glucose joined by α-1,4-linkages
β-D-fructose joined by β-1,2-linkages
α-D-glucose joined by α-1,6-linkages exclusively
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a straight-chain polymer of β-D-glucose units joined by β-1,4-glycosidic linkages; humans lack the enzyme needed to hydrolyse this linkage.
questions.hint: The human digestive system lacks the enzyme for this particular glycosidic configuration.
distractor_logic: This describes starch, specifically its amylose fraction, which humans can digest.
This is not the composition of cellulose; cellulose is built from glucose, not fructose.
Exclusive α-1,6 linkage describes neither cellulose nor the dominant linkage pattern of starch or glycogen chains.

questions.question: Glycogen is sometimes called 'animal starch' because it:
options: Is the storage polysaccharide in animals, structurally similar to but more highly branched than amylopectin
Is a straight, unbranched chain of β-D-glucose units
Cannot be broken down to release glucose in the body
Is found only in plant seeds, like starch
questions.explanation: Like amylopectin, glycogen is a branched α-D-glucose polymer, but with even more frequent branching; it is the glucose-storage polysaccharide in animal liver and muscle.
questions.hint: Think about which organism stores this polysaccharide and how its branching compares to amylopectin.
distractor_logic: Glycogen is highly branched and built from α-D-glucose units, not a straight, β-linked chain.
Glycogen's biological role is precisely to be broken down to release glucose as an energy reserve.
Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide (liver and muscle), whereas starch is the plant storage polysaccharide.

questions.question: Amino acids used to build proteins are, structurally, always:
options: Amino acids with two amino groups and no carboxyl group
α-amino acids, in which the amino group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group
Amino acids with no carboxyl group
β-amino acids, in which the amino group is two carbons away from the carboxyl group
questions.explanation: Naturally occurring amino acids that make up proteins are α-amino acids: the -NH<sub>2</sub> group sits on the carbon directly next to the -COOH group.
questions.hint: The Greek-letter prefix refers to the position of the amino group relative to the carboxyl carbon.
distractor_logic: This matches neither the general definition nor the standard protein-building amino acids, which require both an amino and a carboxyl group.
Every amino acid, by definition, carries at least one carboxyl group along with an amino group.
Proteins are built from α-amino acids, not β-amino acids.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes an essential amino acid from a non-essential one?
options: Essential amino acids do not form peptide bonds
Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained through diet
Essential amino acids are basic, while non-essential amino acids are acidic
Essential amino acids are found only in plant proteins
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids, such as valine and leucine, cannot be synthesised by the body and must be supplied by diet, while non-essential amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, can be synthesised internally.
questions.hint: Focus on the dietary meaning of the word 'essential.'
distractor_logic: All amino acids used in proteins, essential or not, form peptide bonds in the same way.
Essentiality concerns whether the body can synthesise the amino acid, not the acidic or basic character of its side chain.
Essential amino acids must be supplied through diet from any protein source, plant or animal, not exclusively from plants.

questions.question: In the solid state and in aqueous solution, amino acids largely exist as:
options: Free radicals with an unpaired electron on the alpha-carbon
Zwitterions, dipolar ions with -NH<sub>3</sub>+ and -COO− groups
Neutral, fully covalent molecules with intact -NH<sub>2</sub> and -COOH groups
Anions only, with no positive charge anywhere on the molecule
questions.explanation: Amino acids exist as zwitterions, or internal salts, with a protonated amino group and a deprotonated carboxyl group, which also explains their relatively high melting points and water solubility.
questions.hint: Recall the internal proton transfer between the amino and carboxyl groups.
distractor_logic: Amino acids are not free radicals under normal physiological or solid-state conditions.
This ignores the well-documented dipolar, zwitterionic nature of amino acids in these states.
The zwitterion carries both a positive (-NH<sub>3</sub>+) and a negative (-COO−) site simultaneously, not a purely anionic charge.

questions.question: A peptide bond is the linkage formed between:
options: The -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH<sub>2</sub> group of another, with the loss of a water molecule
The side-chain R-groups of two amino acids
The -NH<sub>2</sub> groups of two amino acids, with the loss of ammonia
Two -COOH groups of adjacent amino acids, with the loss of carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: A peptide (amide) bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next amino acid, eliminating a molecule of water.
questions.hint: Think of it as a condensation reaction between -COOH and -NH<sub>2</sub>, similar to ester formation.
distractor_logic: This describes interactions such as disulfide bonds relevant to higher-order protein structure, not the backbone peptide bond itself.
Peptide bond formation requires one -COOH and one -NH<sub>2</sub> group, not two amino groups, and the byproduct is water, not ammonia.
Peptide bond formation involves a -COOH and an -NH<sub>2</sub> group, not two carboxyl groups, and it releases water, not carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Fibrous proteins such as keratin and myosin are characterised by:
options: Chains coiled into a compact spherical shape, generally soluble in water
Being composed exclusively of essential amino acids
Polypeptide chains lying parallel along an axis, held by hydrogen or disulfide bonds, giving long thread-like, water-insoluble structures
A complete absence of secondary structure
questions.explanation: Fibrous proteins have polypeptide chains running parallel, cross-linked by hydrogen and disulfide bonds, giving long, thread-like, water-insoluble structures such as keratin in hair and myosin in muscle.
questions.hint: Think about the overall shape implied by the word 'fibrous.'
distractor_logic: This describes globular proteins, not fibrous proteins.
The essential/non-essential classification of the constituent amino acids is unrelated to whether a protein is classified as fibrous or globular.
Fibrous proteins are in fact defined by extensive, regular secondary structure, not by its absence.

questions.question: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
options: The three-dimensional folding of the polypeptide arising from R-group interactions
The regular shapes, helix or pleated sheet, adopted by a single polypeptide chain
The exact sequence in which amino acids are linked through peptide bonds along the polypeptide chain
The arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits relative to each other
questions.explanation: Primary structure is simply the linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain, which ultimately dictates all higher levels of protein structure.
questions.hint: 'Primary' here refers to the most basic level: the order of building blocks.
distractor_logic: This describes tertiary structure, not primary structure.
This describes secondary structure, not primary structure.
This describes quaternary structure, not primary structure.

questions.question: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet are examples of which level of protein structure?
options: Quaternary structure
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
Primary structure
questions.explanation: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet are the two major secondary-structure patterns, stabilised by hydrogen bonding between the C=O and N-H groups of the peptide backbone.
questions.hint: These two shapes are stabilised mainly by hydrogen bonds along the peptide backbone.
distractor_logic: Quaternary structure concerns the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits, not the local folding pattern of a single chain.
Tertiary structure is the overall 3-D folding of a single chain, built from combinations of secondary-structure elements, not the elements themselves.
Primary structure refers to amino acid sequence, not the regular shapes a chain folds into.

questions.question: Chemically, almost all enzymes are:
options: Nucleic acids
Steroid hormones
Carbohydrates
Globular proteins
questions.explanation: Enzymes are almost exclusively globular proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up specific biochemical reactions.
questions.hint: Recall the general shape category of catalytically active biological proteins.
distractor_logic: The enzymes described in this chapter are globular proteins, not nucleic acids.
Enzymes are biocatalysts built from proteins; steroid hormones are a separate class of chemical messengers.
Enzymes are proteins; carbohydrates are not the catalytically active biomolecules described here.

questions.question: Enzyme names commonly end in the suffix '-ase', which is typically added to the name of:
options: The organ that secretes the enzyme
The vitamin from which the enzyme is synthesised
The temperature at which the enzyme works best
The substrate on which the enzyme acts, or the type of reaction it catalyses
questions.explanation: Enzyme names are usually formed by adding '-ase' to the substrate or reaction type, for example maltase acts on maltose and urease acts on urea.
questions.hint: Think of examples like 'maltase' and 'urease' and what part of the word changes.
distractor_logic: Enzyme names generally reflect what they act on, not which organ produces them.
Enzyme naming is tied to substrate or reaction type, not to a vitamin precursor.
Enzyme nomenclature has nothing to do with its optimal operating temperature.

questions.question: The 'lock and key' model of enzyme action describes:
options: The breakdown of the enzyme itself into simpler amino acids during the reaction
The random collision of any substrate with any enzyme in solution
The permanent, irreversible binding of substrate to enzyme
The complementary fit between an enzyme's active site and its specific substrate, forming an enzyme-substrate complex
questions.explanation: In the lock-and-key model, the enzyme's active site has a shape complementary to a specific substrate, allowing formation of an enzyme-substrate complex that leads to product formation.
questions.hint: The metaphor compares the substrate to a key that fits one particular lock.
distractor_logic: The enzyme is regenerated unchanged after catalysis; it is not consumed or broken down.
The lock-and-key model emphasises specific structural complementarity, not random, non-specific collisions.
In this model, the enzyme-substrate complex forms, reacts, and releases product, regenerating the free enzyme; the binding is not permanent.

questions.question: Vitamins are broadly classified into two solubility-based groups. These are:
options: Natural vitamins and synthetic vitamins
Fat-soluble vitamins and water-soluble vitamins
Essential vitamins and non-essential vitamins
Acidic vitamins and basic vitamins
questions.explanation: Vitamins are classified as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B-group and C) based on their solubility, which also determines how they are stored or excreted by the body.
questions.hint: The classification is based on a physical solubility property.
distractor_logic: This distinguishes source or origin, not the chemical solubility classification used to group vitamins in the chapter.
Unlike amino acids, all vitamins are, by definition, required from external sources; the classification used in this chapter is based on solubility, not essentiality.
Vitamins are not classified by acid-base character; the standard classification is solubility-based.

questions.question: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with scurvy?
options: Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Vitamin A
Vitamin K
questions.explanation: Deficiency of Vitamin C causes scurvy, characterised by bleeding gums and slow wound healing; Vitamin C is also the most easily destroyed vitamin during cooking and storage.
questions.hint: This vitamin is abundant in citrus fruits and amla, and is easily lost on cooking.
distractor_logic: Vitamin D deficiency is linked to rickets or osteomalacia, not scurvy.
Vitamin A deficiency is linked to xerophthalmia (night blindness), not scurvy.
Vitamin K deficiency is linked to increased blood-clotting time, not scurvy.

questions.question: Unlike most vitamins, which of the following is not obtained mainly through diet because the body can synthesise it under suitable conditions?
options: Vitamin A
Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Vitamin B12
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is unusual in that it can be synthesised in the skin on exposure to sunlight, in addition to being obtained from the diet.
questions.hint: Recall which vitamin's synthesis is linked to sunlight exposure on skin.
distractor_logic: Vitamin A must be supplied through diet, such as fish liver oil, carrots, and milk; the body does not synthesise it.
Vitamin C is not synthesised by the human body and must come entirely from the diet.
Vitamin B12 must be obtained from the diet, such as meat, fish, and egg; the body cannot synthesise it.

questions.question: Water-soluble vitamins such as most B-group vitamins must be supplied regularly in the diet mainly because:
options: They cannot cross the intestinal wall unless taken daily
They are not stored in the body to any appreciable extent, unlike fat-soluble vitamins, and excess is excreted in urine
They are toxic if stored in the liver
The body destroys all water-soluble vitamins within minutes of intake
questions.explanation: Because water-soluble vitamins are largely not stored in the body and any excess is excreted through urine, they must be supplied regularly through diet, unlike fat-soluble vitamins, which are stored in the liver and adipose tissue.
questions.hint: Compare how fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins are handled once absorbed.
distractor_logic: Absorption occurs normally; the issue is that the body does not retain a stored reserve of most water-soluble vitamins.
The reason regular supply is needed is lack of storage and excretion, not toxicity from storage.
This overstates the case; the real reason for regular dietary supply is minimal storage and renal excretion, not near-instant destruction.

questions.question: A nucleoside is formed by the attachment of a nitrogenous base to a pentose sugar. What additional component converts a nucleoside into a nucleotide?
options: A phosphate group, esterified typically at the 5' position of the sugar
A second pentose sugar
A second nitrogenous base
A fatty acid chain
questions.explanation: A nucleoside, made of base and sugar, becomes a nucleotide when a phosphate group is attached, typically through an ester linkage at the 5'-carbon of the sugar.
questions.hint: Think of the third structural component of a nucleotide, alongside base and sugar.
distractor_logic: Nucleotides contain a single sugar unit per nucleotide, not two.
A nucleotide contains one base per unit, not two; the additional component is a phosphate group.
Fatty acids are unrelated to nucleotide structure; the missing component is phosphoric acid.

questions.question: Which pentose sugar is present in DNA, distinguishing it from RNA?
options: β-D-2-deoxyribose
β-D-ribose
β-D-glucose
β-D-fructose
questions.explanation: DNA contains β-D-2-deoxyribose, lacking an -OH at the 2' position, while RNA contains β-D-ribose.
questions.hint: The name of this sugar reflects the 'missing' oxygen at one carbon compared to ribose.
distractor_logic: This is the sugar found in RNA, not DNA.
Neither DNA nor RNA contains glucose as its backbone sugar; both use five-carbon sugars.
Fructose is a ketohexose found in carbohydrates such as sucrose, not a component of nucleic acids.

questions.question: Which nitrogenous base is found in DNA but not in RNA?
options: Thymine
Guanine
Cytosine
Adenine
questions.explanation: Thymine is unique to DNA; RNA has uracil in its place, while adenine, guanine, and cytosine are common to both nucleic acids.
questions.hint: Three of the four common bases are shared between DNA and RNA; only one differs.
distractor_logic: Guanine is present in both DNA and RNA.
Cytosine is present in both DNA and RNA.
Adenine is present in both DNA and RNA.

questions.question: In the Watson-Crick double helix, successive nucleotides within a single strand are linked to each other through:
options: Peptide bonds between adjacent sugar units
Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases on the same strand
Glycosidic bonds between adjacent phosphate groups
3'-5' phosphodiester linkages forming the sugar-phosphate backbone
questions.explanation: Within each polynucleotide strand, adjacent nucleotides are covalently joined through 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds, forming the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone.
questions.hint: Distinguish the bond that holds the backbone together from the bond that pairs the two strands.
distractor_logic: Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins; nucleotides within a strand are linked by phosphodiester bonds.
Hydrogen bonding occurs between bases on opposite strands during base pairing, not between successive nucleotides on the same strand.
The base-sugar bond is the glycosidic bond; successive nucleotides are joined through phosphodiester, not glycosidic, linkages.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: DNA replication is described as 'semi-conservative' because:
options: Each daughter DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
DNA replication occurs only in half the cells of an organism
Both daughter DNA molecules are made entirely of new material, with the parent strands discarded
Only half of the DNA molecule is copied during each round of cell division
questions.explanation: In semi-conservative replication, the two parental strands separate and each serves as a template for a new complementary strand, so each resulting DNA molecule retains exactly one original strand.
questions.hint: Focus on what each of the two new DNA molecules retains from the original molecule.
distractor_logic: This concerns which cells undergo replication, unrelated to the meaning of 'semi-conservative' at the molecular level.
This would describe a fully non-conservative model, not the semi-conservative model that actually operates.
The entire DNA molecule is duplicated; 'semi-conservative' refers to strand origin in the daughter molecules, not incomplete copying.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: The sequence of bases along a DNA strand constitutes the genetic code because it ultimately determines:
options: The solubility of the DNA molecule in water
The sequence of amino acids in the proteins synthesised by the cell
The colour of the cell membrane
The number of phosphate groups in each nucleotide
questions.explanation: The base sequence of DNA is transcribed into mRNA and then translated into a specific sequence of amino acids, which is why DNA is considered the carrier of genetic information.
questions.hint: Trace the flow from DNA base sequence to the final biomolecule it specifies.
distractor_logic: DNA's general solubility is not what is meant by its role as the genetic code; the code specifically governs protein amino-acid sequence.
This is not a property that base sequence is described as determining in this chapter.
Each nucleotide has essentially the same phosphate arrangement regardless of base identity; base sequence is what varies and carries genetic information.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: Which biomolecule directly carries the genetic message from DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome for protein synthesis?
options: t-RNA
DNA itself, which leaves the nucleus to reach the ribosome
r-RNA
m-RNA
questions.explanation: Messenger RNA is synthesised as a complementary copy of a DNA segment through transcription and carries this genetic message out of the nucleus to the ribosome for translation.
questions.hint: The name of this RNA type describes its function directly.
distractor_logic: t-RNA's role is to bring specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation, not to carry the genetic message from DNA.
DNA remains in the nucleus; it is transcribed into mRNA, which then travels to the ribosome.
r-RNA is a structural and functional component of the ribosome itself, not the messenger carrying the code from DNA.

questions.question: Hormones act as chemical messengers that are:
options: Secreted by endocrine glands directly into the bloodstream and transported to a distant site of action
Enzymes that catalyse digestion of food within the gut
Structural proteins found only in connective tissue
Secreted only by the pancreas, regardless of their target organ
questions.explanation: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly into the blood by endocrine glands, which then act on target cells or organs elsewhere in the body.
questions.hint: Focus on how the messenger travels from its gland of origin to its site of action.
distractor_logic: This describes digestive enzymes, not hormones, which serve as intercellular messengers rather than localised digestive catalysts.
Hormones are chemical messengers of varied classes, steroid, peptide, or amino-acid derivative, not structural proteins.
Many different endocrine glands, including the thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, and gonads, secrete different hormones, not the pancreas exclusively.

questions.question: Insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose level, is chemically classified as a:
options: Peptide or protein hormone
Steroid
Amino-acid derivative like adrenaline
Carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Insulin is a peptide hormone, secreted by the β-cells of the pancreas, that helps regulate blood glucose levels; its deficiency or malfunction is linked to diabetes.
questions.hint: Insulin is built from amino acid chains, like other protein hormones.
distractor_logic: Steroid hormones, such as estrogen and testosterone, are derived from cholesterol; insulin is not a steroid.
Amino-acid-derivative hormones are small molecules derived from a single amino acid; insulin is a polypeptide made of multiple linked amino acids.
Insulin is composed of amino acids, not sugar units; it is a protein, not a carbohydrate.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a hormone with its chemical class?
options: Oxytocin – steroid hormone
Adrenaline – steroid hormone
Thyroxine – steroid hormone
Testosterone – steroid hormone
questions.explanation: Testosterone, like estrogen and progesterone, is a steroid hormone derived from cholesterol, whereas adrenaline and thyroxine are amino-acid derivatives and oxytocin is a peptide hormone.
questions.hint: Recall which hormones are built on a cholesterol-derived steroid skeleton versus an amino-acid backbone.
distractor_logic: Oxytocin is a small peptide hormone, not a steroid.
Adrenaline is an amino-acid-derivative hormone, not a steroid.
Thyroxine is an iodine-containing amino-acid-derivative hormone, not a steroid.

questions.question: A carbohydrate gives a negative Tollens' test in its intact form. On acid hydrolysis, it yields exactly two different monosaccharides in equal amounts, each of which individually gives a positive Tollens' test. This behaviour is characteristic of:
options: Glucose, a monosaccharide
Sucrose, a non-reducing disaccharide
Starch, a polysaccharide
Cellulose, a polysaccharide
questions.explanation: This pattern, non-reducing in the intact form and exactly two different reducing monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, matches sucrose, which hydrolyses to glucose and fructose via a linkage that uses both anomeric carbons.
questions.hint: Focus on both 'two different units' and 'equal amounts' as clues about which specific disaccharide this must be.
distractor_logic: Monosaccharides do not need hydrolysis to show reducing behaviour; they are reducing sugars by themselves.
Hydrolysis of starch yields a very large number of units of a single monosaccharide, glucose, not exactly two different monosaccharides in equal amounts.
Hydrolysis of cellulose yields a very large number of glucose units, not exactly two different monosaccharides.

questions.question: Maltose gives a positive Fehling's test, while sucrose does not. Based on the number of anomeric carbons engaged in the glycosidic bond, what can be concluded?
options: In maltose, both anomeric carbons participate in the glycosidic bond, but in sucrose, neither does
Neither maltose nor sucrose has any anomeric carbon involved in its glycosidic bond
The number of anomeric carbons involved has no bearing on reducing behaviour
In maltose, only one of the two anomeric carbons participates in the glycosidic bond, but in sucrose, both anomeric carbons participate
questions.explanation: Maltose retains one free anomeric -OH, since only one anomeric carbon is used in its α-1,4 linkage, so it can still open to a reactive carbonyl form and reduce Fehling's solution, whereas sucrose ties up both anomeric carbons.
questions.hint: Compare how many anomeric carbons are consumed in forming each glycosidic bond.
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual situation; sucrose is the sugar in which both anomeric carbons are engaged in the linkage.
This contradicts the very definition of a glycosidic bond, which is always formed using at least one anomeric carbon.
This directly contradicts the given data, since the differing Fehling's test outcomes trace exactly to how many anomeric carbons are tied up in each linkage.

questions.question: A student is given an unknown white solid and told it is a carbohydrate. On testing, it gives a positive iodine test (blue-black colour) but is insoluble in cold water and does not reduce Fehling's solution. This unknown is most likely:
options: Starch, a polysaccharide
Cellulose, a polysaccharide
Glucose, a monosaccharide
Sucrose, a disaccharide
questions.explanation: The blue-black colour with iodine is a specific test for starch, arising from iodine trapped inside the amylose helix; combined with water-insolubility and lack of reducing character, this points to starch rather than a mono- or disaccharide.
questions.hint: The colour reaction with iodine is a defining test for one particular polysaccharide.
distractor_logic: Cellulose does not give the characteristic blue-black colour with iodine, since that reaction is specific to starch's amylose helix.
Glucose is water-soluble, reduces Fehling's solution, and does not give the characteristic blue-black colour with iodine that starch does.
Sucrose is water-soluble and does not give the iodine colour test, which is specific to starch's helical amylose component.

questions.question: Glucose does not give the characteristic 2,4-DNP test for a carbonyl group and does not react appreciably with sodium bisulfite (NaHSO<sub>3</sub>), even though its open-chain form has a free -CHO group. What does this observation, together with mutarotation, best support?
options: That glucose cannot be oxidised under any conditions
That glucose predominantly exists in a cyclic hemiacetal form rather than as a free open-chain aldehyde
That glucose is a ketone, not an aldehyde
That glucose does not actually contain an aldehyde group at all
questions.explanation: The failure of glucose to give a strong 2,4-DNP or bisulfite response, along with its mutarotation behaviour, indicates that in solution glucose exists predominantly as a cyclic hemiacetal, with the -CHO tied up as part of the ring, rather than as the free open-chain aldehyde.
questions.hint: Think about which form of glucose, open-chain or ring, would react readily with carbonyl-specific reagents.
distractor_logic: Glucose is in fact oxidised by mild oxidants such as bromine water to gluconic acid; these particular tests concern carbonyl-specific reagents, not oxidisability in general.
Glucose is an aldohexose; these tests probe why its aldehyde character seems muted in solution, not whether it is secretly a ketone.

Other evidence, such as oxime formation and oxidation to gluconic acid, confirms glucose does have a -CHO group in its open-chain form; the point here is that this form is not the predominant species in solution.

questions.question: Freshly prepared α-D-glucose has a specific rotation of about +112°, which gradually changes on standing in solution to an equilibrium value of about +52.5°. This phenomenon, mutarotation, occurs because:
options: Glucose reacts with atmospheric oxygen to form gluconic acid over time
Glucose slowly decomposes into carbon dioxide and water on standing
α-D-glucose interconverts, through the open-chain form, with β-D-glucose until an equilibrium mixture of the two anomers is reached
Light exposure irreversibly converts glucose into fructose
questions.explanation: Mutarotation arises because the cyclic hemiacetal ring of glucose can open back to the open-chain aldehyde form and reclose, allowing interconversion between the α and β anomers until a stable equilibrium mixture is reached.
questions.hint: The specific rotation is changing because one anomer is slowly converting into a mixture with the other, not because the molecule is being destroyed.
distractor_logic: This describes an oxidation reaction, not the reversible ring-opening and ring-closing equilibrium responsible for mutarotation.
Mutarotation is a reversible interconversion between anomeric forms, not decomposition of the glucose molecule.
Mutarotation has nothing to do with light or with conversion into a different sugar; it is an interconversion between the two anomers of the same sugar.

questions.question: α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose are described as anomers. What structural feature specifically distinguishes them?
options: The configuration of the -OH group at the anomeric carbon, C1, which is newly created on ring closure
The total number of carbon atoms in the ring
Whether the sugar is D- or L-configured
The configuration of the -OH group at C5, the ring-oxygen-bearing carbon
questions.explanation: Anomers of glucose differ only in the spatial configuration at the anomeric carbon, C1, which becomes a new stereocentre when the open-chain form cyclises; all other stereocentres remain unchanged.
questions.hint: The anomeric carbon is the one that is newly generated as a stereocentre during ring closure.
distractor_logic: Both anomers are six-membered pyranose rings built from the same six carbons; they do not differ in ring size or carbon count.
Both α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose belong to the D-series; the anomeric distinction concerns C1 configuration, not the D/L descriptor, which is fixed by the configuration at C5.
The C5 configuration is fixed and shared by both anomers; it is the newly formed stereocentre at C1 that differs between the α and β forms.

questions.question: When glucose is reduced with HI (hydroiodic acid), the product obtained is n-hexane, a straight-chain hydrocarbon with no branching. What does this specifically establish about the carbon skeleton of glucose?
options: Glucose exists predominantly as a six-membered ring in solution
Glucose contains a free aldehyde group
Glucose contains exactly five hydroxyl groups
All six carbon atoms of glucose are joined in a single continuous, unbranched chain
questions.explanation: Since exhaustive reduction of glucose with HI removes all the oxygen-bearing functional groups and yields unbranched n-hexane, this confirms that the six carbons of glucose form a single straight chain with no branching.
questions.hint: Focus on what 'no branching in the reduction product' tells you about carbon connectivity, independent of oxygen-containing groups.
distractor_logic: Reduction to n-hexane removes all oxygen functionality and collapses any ring back to an open chain, demonstrating underlying carbon connectivity rather than the predominant solution-phase ring form.

Oxime formation and oxidation to gluconic acid establish the aldehyde group; complete reduction to n-hexane instead confirms the shape of the carbon backbone once all oxygen-containing groups are removed.
The pentaacetate test, not HI reduction, is what establishes the number of -OH groups; HI reduction instead targets the carbon skeleton.

questions.question: Glucose and fructose are both members of the D-family of sugars, even though one is an aldose and the other is a ketose. This D/L classification is based on:
options: Whether the sugar's carbonyl group is an aldehyde or a ketone
The number of carbon atoms in the sugar's chain
Whether the sugar rotates plane-polarised light to the right (D) or left (L)
The configuration of the -OH group at the highest-numbered chiral carbon, compared with the reference compound D- or L-glyceraldehyde
questions.explanation: The D/L descriptor is assigned by comparing the configuration at the highest-numbered chiral carbon, the one nearest the terminal -CH<sub>2</sub>OH, to D- or L-glyceraldehyde, independent of whether the sugar is an aldose or ketose.
questions.hint: Recall that D/L is a configurational label tied to a reference molecule, not a description of the carbonyl group or the observed rotation direction.
distractor_logic: Aldose versus ketose describes the carbonyl type, an entirely separate classification from the D/L configurational descriptor.
D/L classification is unrelated to chain length; both pentoses and hexoses can independently be D- or L-configured.
D/L is a configurational descriptor tied to glyceraldehyde, not a direct statement of the observed direction of optical rotation, which is instead denoted by (+) or (−).

questions.question: On hydrolysis, sucrose gives an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose called invert sugar, and this mixture is laevorotatory overall even though sucrose itself is dextrorotatory. What best explains this net change in optical rotation?
options: Hydrolysis destroys the optical activity of both sugars, and the laevorotation is a measurement error
Fructose's large laevorotation (about −92°) outweighs glucose's smaller dextrorotation (about +52°) in the equimolar mixture
Glucose becomes laevorotatory upon hydrolysis of sucrose
Fructose is formed in a much larger quantity than glucose during hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Since fructose's specific rotation, about −92°, is much larger in magnitude than glucose's, about +52°, even an equimolar mixture of the two ends up net laevorotatory, explaining the name 'invert sugar' for the reversal in sign of rotation upon hydrolysis.
questions.hint: Compare the magnitudes, not just the signs, of glucose's and fructose's individual specific rotations.
distractor_logic: Both glucose and fructose remain optically active after hydrolysis; the laevorotation of the mixture is a real, well-documented net effect, not an artefact.
Glucose itself remains dextrorotatory after hydrolysis; the net sign change arises because fructose's strong laevorotation dominates the mixture.
Hydrolysis of sucrose gives an equimolar, 1:1 mixture of glucose and fructose, not an excess of one over the other; the sign change is due to the relative magnitude of each sugar's specific rotation.

questions.question: Both glucose and fructose reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent, and both give the same osazone (glucosazone) with excess phenylhydrazine. What does this shared osazone result specifically indicate about the two sugars' structures?
options: Glucose and fructose have identical configurations at all carbons except C1 and C2, since osazone formation involves only these first two carbons
The shared osazone indicates both sugars have five hydroxyl groups
Osazone formation proves that fructose does not contain a ketone group
Glucose and fructose are actually the same molecule with two different names
questions.explanation: Since osazone formation involves only C1 and C2 of a sugar, glucose and fructose giving the identical glucosazone shows that their structures beyond C2, at C3, C4, C5, and C6, must be identical.
questions.hint: Recall which carbons are chemically altered during osazone formation, and think about what an identical product implies about the rest of the molecule.
distractor_logic: Osazone formation specifically involves the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent hydroxyl-bearing carbon reacting with phenylhydrazine, not a general count of hydroxyl groups across the whole molecule.
Fructose does contain a ketone group; osazone formation is precisely the reaction that derivatises that ketone group and the adjacent -CH<sub>2</sub>OH, alongside the aldehyde in glucose's case.
Glucose and fructose are distinct sugars, an aldohexose and a ketohexose respectively, differing in the position and type of their carbonyl group; they are not identical.

questions.question: A sample is hydrolysed and found to yield only glucose, with no other monosaccharide detected, regardless of the reaction time. Also, before hydrolysis, the sample already gives a positive Fehling's test. Which disaccharide fits this description?
options: Lactose
Sucrose
Maltose
