A disaccharide formed purely from β-linked fructose units
questions.explanation: Maltose is composed of two glucose units joined by an α-1,4-glycosidic bond, so its only hydrolysis product is glucose, and because one anomeric carbon remains free, it also directly gives a positive Fehling's test.
questions.hint: Identify which of the three common disaccharides is built from only one type of monosaccharide unit and is also reducing.
distractor_logic: Lactose hydrolyses to give glucose and galactose, not glucose alone.
Sucrose hydrolyses to give both glucose and fructose, not glucose alone, and sucrose itself does not give a positive Fehling's test before hydrolysis.
This is not one of the three disaccharides discussed in the chapter, and disaccharides built purely from fructose are not part of the standard syllabus scope here.

questions.question: A disaccharide is found to yield glucose and galactose on hydrolysis and also reduces Fehling's solution in its intact form. This disaccharide must be:
options: Sucrose
Maltose
Lactose
Starch
questions.explanation: Lactose, the sugar found in milk, hydrolyses to give one unit of galactose and one unit of glucose, and because one anomeric carbon remains free, it is a reducing sugar.
questions.hint: Among the three common disaccharides, only one pairs glucose with galactose.
distractor_logic: Sucrose yields glucose and fructose, not galactose, on hydrolysis.
Maltose yields two units of glucose, not glucose plus galactose.
Starch yields many units of glucose alone on complete hydrolysis, not a glucose-galactose pair, and it is a polysaccharide, not a disaccharide.

questions.question: If the α-1,4-glycosidic linkage of maltose were somehow converted to a β-1,4-glycosidic linkage between the same two glucose units, which property would most directly be affected first?
options: The classification of the compound from a carbohydrate to a protein
The stereochemical configuration at the linking anomeric carbon, changing how the resulting disaccharide is recognised and processed by enzymes
The number of monosaccharide units obtained on hydrolysis, which would increase from two to three
The molecular formula of the disaccharide, which would gain extra oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: The α/β designation of a glycosidic linkage is a matter of stereochemical configuration at the anomeric carbon; switching it does not change the molecular formula or the hydrolysis-unit count, but it does change how enzymes recognise and process the linkage, as seen in the contrast between α-linked, digestible starch and β-linked, indigestible cellulose.
questions.hint: Think about what actually changes when only the spatial arrangement at one stereocentre is altered, versus what stays the same.
distractor_logic: Changing the stereochemistry of the glycosidic linkage does not alter the fundamental chemical class of the compound, which remains a carbohydrate.
Hydrolysis of a disaccharide, regardless of α or β linkage, still yields exactly two monosaccharide units.
Changing α to β only alters the spatial orientation at the anomeric carbon; it does not add or remove atoms, so the molecular formula stays the same.

questions.question: Amylose gives a deep blue colour with iodine, while amylopectin gives a reddish-purple colour. What structural feature of amylose is primarily responsible for its characteristic blue colour with iodine?
options: Its solubility in cold water
Its extensive branching at α-1,6 positions
Its long, unbranched helical chain, which can trap iodine molecules within the coil
Its composition of β-D-glucose units
questions.explanation: Amylose's unbranched chain coils into a helix, and iodine molecules become trapped within this helical structure, producing the characteristic deep blue colour; amylopectin's branched structure does not form as regular a helix, giving a different colour.
questions.hint: Think about the shape that an unbranched polysaccharide chain can adopt, and what that shape can trap inside it.
distractor_logic: Solubility behaviour is a separate physical property from the mechanism of the iodine colour test, which depends specifically on the helical shape trapping iodine.
Extensive branching is a feature of amylopectin, not amylose, and is associated with the different, reddish-purple, colour reaction.
Both amylose and amylopectin, like all of starch, are composed of α-D-glucose units, not β-D-glucose.

questions.question: A student compares three polysaccharides, starch, cellulose, and glycogen, on the basis of the glycosidic linkages used and the degree of branching. Which correctly ranks them from least branched to most branched?
options: Glycogen (unbranched) < starch < cellulose (highly branched)
Cellulose (unbranched) < starch, specifically amylopectin (moderately branched) < glycogen (highly branched)
All three polysaccharides have exactly the same degree of branching
Starch (unbranched) < cellulose < glycogen (highly branched)
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a straight, unbranched chain of β-D-glucose; starch, through its amylopectin fraction, is moderately branched with α-1,6 branch points; and glycogen has even more frequent branching than amylopectin, reflecting its role as a rapidly mobilisable energy store.
questions.hint: Recall which of the three is used purely as a structural material versus which two are storage forms that benefit from more branching.
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual pattern; glycogen is the most highly branched of the three, and cellulose is unbranched, not the most branched.
This ignores clear structural differences: cellulose is a straight chain, amylopectin has moderate branching, and glycogen is even more extensively branched than amylopectin.
Cellulose, not starch, is the unbranched one among the three; starch's amylopectin component is already moderately branched.

questions.question: A plant polysaccharide sample gives a positive iodine test but is only partially hydrolysed by amylase, leaving a resistant, more highly branched core. This resistant core most likely corresponds to regions rich in:
options: α-1,4 linkages only
α-1,6 branch points
Peptide bonds within the polysaccharide chain
β-1,4 linkages, as in cellulose
questions.explanation: The branch points in amylopectin are formed by α-1,6-glycosidic linkages, which many amylases act on less efficiently than the straight-chain α-1,4 linkages, so branched regions tend to resist complete enzymatic hydrolysis.
questions.hint: Recall which type of linkage specifically creates the branch points in a partially branched glucose polymer.
distractor_logic: Amylase readily acts on straight-chain α-1,4 linkages; a linkage type that amylase struggles with is more consistent with resistant branch points, not with the linkage it hydrolyses easily.
Polysaccharides are built from glycosidic linkages between sugar units, not peptide bonds, which are specific to proteins.
Starch, unlike cellulose, is composed of α-linked glucose units throughout, so β-1,4 linkages would not be present in a starch sample at all.

questions.question: Glycine is the only common amino acid that lacks optical activity. What structural feature of glycine explains this?
options: It has an aromatic side chain that cancels out optical rotation
It has no carboxyl group
Its alpha-carbon bears two hydrogen atoms rather than four different groups, so it is not a chiral centre
It exists only in the D-form, never the L-form
questions.explanation: For a carbon to be a stereocentre, it must bear four different groups; glycine's alpha-carbon carries -NH<sub>2</sub>, -COOH, and two identical -H atoms, so it is not chiral, and glycine has no optical activity.
questions.hint: Check whether all four groups attached to glycine's alpha-carbon are actually different from one another.
distractor_logic: Glycine's side chain is simply a hydrogen atom, not an aromatic ring; its lack of chirality is due to the duplicated hydrogen substituents on the alpha-carbon.
Glycine, like every amino acid, does have a carboxyl group; its lack of chirality is due to the identity of the groups on the alpha-carbon, not the absence of -COOH.
The D/L distinction applies only to chiral amino acids; because glycine's alpha-carbon is not a stereocentre at all, it cannot be assigned to either the D- or L-series.

questions.question: Glutamic acid has two carboxyl groups and one amino group, while lysine has one carboxyl group and two amino groups. Based on this, how would these two amino acids be classified?
options: Both as neutral amino acids, since each has at least one of each functional group
Both as essential amino acids, based on their functional group count
Glutamic acid as an acidic amino acid, and lysine as a basic amino acid
Glutamic acid as a basic amino acid, and lysine as an acidic amino acid
questions.explanation: Amino acids with an excess of carboxyl groups over amino groups, like glutamic acid, are classified as acidic, while those with an excess of amino groups over carboxyl groups, like lysine, are classified as basic.
questions.hint: Compare the relative count of -NH<sub>2</sub> versus -COOH groups in each amino acid to decide its acid-base classification.
distractor_logic: Neutral classification applies specifically when the numbers of -NH<sub>2</sub> and -COOH groups are equal; here they are unequal in both amino acids, giving each a net acidic or basic character.
Essential versus non-essential classification is based on whether the body can synthesise the amino acid, which is unrelated to how many -NH<sub>2</sub> or -COOH groups it carries.
This reverses the actual assignment; the amino acid with the extra carboxyl group is acidic, and the one with the extra amino group is basic.

questions.question: At a certain pH, a particular amino acid carries no net electric charge and does not migrate toward either electrode in an electric field, even though it still exists as a zwitterion. This pH is called the amino acid's:
options: Denaturation temperature
Optical rotation angle
Boiling point
Isoelectric point
questions.explanation: The isoelectric point is the specific pH at which an amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion with equal numbers of positive and negative charges, giving it zero net charge and no net migration in an electric field.
questions.hint: This special pH value is defined by a balance between the positively and negatively charged forms of the amino acid.
distractor_logic: Denaturation temperature is a property of proteins losing their higher-order structure, not a pH-related property of an individual amino acid's net charge.
Optical rotation describes how a compound rotates plane-polarised light, not its behaviour in an electric field at a particular pH.
Boiling point is a thermal property unrelated to net charge or migration in an electric field.

questions.question: Two proteins have identical amino acid sequences, but one shows biological activity and the other does not, because only one has folded into its correct three-dimensional shape. This difference in activity is most directly attributable to differences in their:
options: The total molecular weight of the protein
Primary structure, since amino acid sequence alone determines biological activity
The number of essential amino acids present
Tertiary (and possibly secondary) structure, since biological activity typically requires the correctly folded three-dimensional shape
questions.explanation: While primary structure is identical in this scenario, biological activity depends on the protein correctly folding into its native secondary and tertiary structure; a misfolded protein with the same sequence can be biologically inactive.
questions.hint: The two proteins share the same building blocks in the same order; consider what differs when only the folding is different.
distractor_logic: Molecular weight would be identical for two proteins with the same amino acid sequence; the biologically relevant difference described is in shape, not mass.
The scenario specifies that both proteins have identical sequences; the biological activity here depends on how that sequence is folded, not on the sequence itself.
Essential or non-essential status of individual amino acids has no bearing on whether the overall protein has folded correctly.

questions.question: Boiling egg white causes it to coagulate into a solid, opaque mass, and this change cannot be reversed simply by cooling. What is happening to the protein (albumin) at the molecular level?
options: Its secondary and tertiary structure are disrupted by heat, while the primary structure remains intact
Its primary structure is broken, converting the protein into free amino acids
The protein is converted into a carbohydrate through a rearrangement of its atoms
The protein's molecular formula changes because atoms are lost during boiling
questions.explanation: Heat-induced denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that maintain a protein's secondary and tertiary structure, causing it to unfold and often aggregate irreversibly, while the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure remain unaffected.
questions.hint: Distinguish between the covalent backbone of the protein and the weaker interactions responsible for its 3-D shape.
distractor_logic: Denaturation by heat affects the higher-order folding of the protein; the peptide bonds defining the primary sequence are not broken under ordinary boiling conditions.
Denaturation changes a protein's shape, not its fundamental chemical class; albumin remains a protein throughout coagulation.
Denaturation is a conformational change, not a change in the underlying chemical composition or molecular formula of the protein.

questions.question: Haemoglobin is made up of four polypeptide subunits, two α-chains and two β-chains, that must associate correctly for the molecule to function as an oxygen carrier. This level of organisation, describing how separate polypeptide chains are arranged relative to each other, is called:
options: Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
Primary structure
Quaternary structure
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure describes the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits relative to one another; haemoglobin's four subunits assembling into a functional whole is a classic example.
questions.hint: This level of structure specifically applies only to proteins made of more than one polypeptide chain.
distractor_logic: Secondary structure describes local folding patterns like helices or sheets within one chain, not the association of multiple chains.
Tertiary structure describes the 3-D folding of a single polypeptide chain, not how multiple independent chains come together.
Primary structure concerns the amino acid sequence within a single chain, not the arrangement of multiple separate chains.

questions.question: A change in pH away from the physiological range can denature a protein even without any change in temperature. Which explanation best accounts for this pH sensitivity?
options: Changing pH converts the protein's amino acids into carbohydrates
Changing pH has no real effect on protein structure; only temperature can denature a protein
Changing pH breaks all the peptide bonds in the protein instantly
Changing pH alters the ionisation state of acidic and basic side chains, disrupting the ionic and hydrogen-bonding interactions that stabilise the protein's folded shape
questions.explanation: Protein folding depends on a network of ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and other interactions involving charged and polar side chains; shifting the pH changes the protonation state of these groups, disrupting these stabilising interactions and denaturing the protein even without added heat.
questions.hint: Consider how the charge on acidic and basic side chains would change as pH moves away from its optimal range.
distractor_logic: A pH change does not convert one class of biomolecule into another; it affects the charge state and folding of the existing amino acid side chains.
This directly contradicts the premise of the question, and pH-induced denaturation is well documented, such as milk curdling when it becomes acidic.
Peptide bonds are relatively stable covalent bonds and are not instantly broken by ordinary pH shifts; denaturation instead disrupts the weaker interactions maintaining higher-order structure.

questions.question: An enzyme that works efficiently at 37°C shows a sharp drop in activity when the temperature is raised to 70°C, and this loss of activity is not regained on cooling back to 37°C. What has most likely happened to the enzyme?
options: The enzyme's optimal temperature has simply shifted to 70°C and it will work normally there from now on
The enzyme has been converted into a different type of biomolecule by the heat
The enzyme, being a globular protein, has been denatured by heat, destroying the specific shape of its active site
The substrate has been permanently altered so no enzyme could act on it
questions.explanation: Because enzymes are globular proteins, excessive heat denatures them by destroying the precise three-dimensional shape of the active site required for substrate binding, and this loss of activity is generally irreversible.
questions.hint: Recall what class of biomolecule enzymes belong to, and what happens to that class of molecule at high temperatures.
distractor_logic: A sharp drop in activity at high temperature with no recovery on cooling is the classic signature of irreversible denaturation, not a shift in optimal operating temperature.
Heat denaturation changes the enzyme's shape, not its fundamental chemical identity as a protein.
The scenario describes the enzyme's own activity being lost irreversibly, best explained by heat directly affecting the enzyme's own protein structure.

questions.question: A particular enzyme catalyses the hydrolysis of maltose but has no effect on sucrose or lactose, even though all three are disaccharides. This selectivity is best explained by the enzyme's:
options: Random chance in which substrate happens to collide with it
Highly specific active site, which is structurally complementary only to maltose and not to the other disaccharides
Preference for reacting only with non-reducing sugars
Inability to catalyse any hydrolysis reactions at all
questions.explanation: Enzymes are highly specific catalysts; an enzyme like maltase has an active site shaped to fit only maltose, so it does not catalyse the hydrolysis of structurally different disaccharides such as sucrose or lactose.
questions.hint: Recall the defining feature of enzyme action described by the lock-and-key model.
distractor_logic: Enzyme action is governed by specific structural complementarity between active site and substrate, not by random chance, as emphasised by the lock-and-key model.
Maltose, the sugar this enzyme does act on, is itself a reducing sugar, so this explanation does not fit the given data.
The scenario explicitly states the enzyme does catalyse hydrolysis of maltose; the issue is its lack of activity toward the other two sugars, not a general inability to hydrolyse.

questions.question: Two flasks contain the same concentration of an enzyme and its substrate. Flask A is kept at pH 7, the enzyme's optimum, and Flask B is adjusted to pH 2. After the same time interval, Flask A shows much more product formed than Flask B. What does this best illustrate about enzyme activity?
options: Enzymes work equally well at any pH as long as temperature is constant
The substrate itself changed identity at low pH, independent of the enzyme
Enzyme activity is sensitive to pH, and deviation from the optimum pH can reduce catalytic efficiency
Enzymes are completely unaffected by the pH of their surroundings
questions.explanation: Enzymes, being proteins, have an optimum pH at which their active site retains the correct shape for substrate binding; moving away from this optimum, such as to a strongly acidic pH of 2, can reduce or abolish catalytic activity.
questions.hint: Compare the two flasks and identify which single variable was changed between them.
distractor_logic: This contradicts the data given; a sizeable drop in product formation at pH 2 versus pH 7 shows that pH, independent of temperature, strongly affects enzyme activity.
The scenario specifically points to reduced activity under altered pH conditions, consistent with the enzyme's own structure and function being pH-sensitive.
This directly contradicts the outcome described, where a large pH shift clearly reduced product formation.

questions.question: A sailor on a long voyage without access to fresh fruits or vegetables develops bleeding gums and slow wound healing after several weeks. Which dietary deficiency is most consistent with these symptoms?
options: Vitamin A deficiency, since fresh fruits are also a major source of Vitamin A
Vitamin K deficiency, since it also relates to blood
Vitamin C deficiency, since it is the most easily destroyed vitamin and not stored appreciably in the body
Vitamin D deficiency, since sunlight was unavailable at sea
questions.explanation: The symptoms described are classic for scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency; because Vitamin C is not stored well in the body and is readily destroyed by cooking or prolonged storage, diets lacking fresh produce for extended periods commonly lead to this deficiency.
questions.hint: Identify which vitamin is described as the most easily lost from food and not appreciably stored in the body.
distractor_logic: Vitamin A deficiency is specifically linked to xerophthalmia (night blindness), not to bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

Vitamin K deficiency affects blood clotting time, but the classic symptom set described here, bleeding gums plus slow wound healing on long voyages without fresh produce, is specifically scurvy from Vitamin C deficiency.
Sea voyages generally still provide sunlight exposure, and Vitamin D deficiency causes bone-related conditions such as rickets or osteomalacia, not bleeding gums.

questions.question: A person taking very large doses of Vitamin A supplements over a long period risks toxic accumulation, whereas taking similarly large doses of Vitamin C rarely leads to toxic buildup. What general principle about vitamin classes explains this difference?
options: Fat-soluble vitamins like Vitamin A can be stored in the liver and adipose tissue, allowing them to accumulate, while water-soluble vitamins like Vitamin C are readily excreted in urine
Vitamin A is synthesised in the body, while Vitamin C must always be taken as a supplement
Vitamin A is toxic in any amount, while Vitamin C is never toxic under any circumstance
Vitamin C is not actually a vitamin, so it behaves differently
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in the liver and adipose tissue, so excessive intake can accumulate to toxic levels over time, whereas water-soluble vitamins like Vitamin C are largely not stored and any excess is excreted in urine, making toxic accumulation far less common.
questions.hint: Think about how the solubility classification of a vitamin affects whether the body can store it long-term.
distractor_logic: Vitamin A must be obtained through diet, similar to Vitamin C; the accumulation difference is explained by fat-solubility and storage capacity, not by whether the body synthesises the vitamin.
The difference described is about accumulation and storage tendency at high doses, not an absolute toxicity or non-toxicity rule independent of dose.
Vitamin C is a well-established water-soluble vitamin; its different behaviour is explained by its solubility class, not by it being excluded from the vitamin category.

questions.question: A strict vegan diet with no animal products or fortified foods poses a particular long-term risk for deficiency of which vitamin, given its natural dietary sources?
options: Vitamin A
Vitamin K
Vitamin B12
Vitamin C
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12's natural dietary sources are meat, fish, and eggs, so diets that exclude all animal products carry a real long-term risk of B12 deficiency, which can lead to pernicious anaemia.
questions.hint: Recall which vitamin's listed dietary sources are almost exclusively animal-derived.
distractor_logic: Plant sources can supply precursor carotenoids that the body converts to Vitamin A, unlike Vitamin B12, which has essentially no reliable plant source.
Vitamin K is found in green leafy vegetables and can also be produced by intestinal bacteria, so it is not the vitamin most at risk in a plant-based diet.
Vitamin C is abundant in plant sources such as citrus fruits and amla, so a vegan diet does not particularly threaten Vitamin C intake.

questions.question: A child who spends very little time outdoors and has a diet poor in fish and egg yolk develops soft, poorly mineralised bones. Which vitamin deficiency is most directly implicated, and why does limited outdoor time matter here?
options: Vitamin D deficiency, because Vitamin D can be synthesised in the skin on exposure to sunlight, in addition to being obtained from limited dietary sources
Vitamin K deficiency, because Vitamin K is also linked to bone health and sunlight
Vitamin E deficiency, because Vitamin E is fat-soluble like Vitamin D
Vitamin B1 deficiency, because B1 deficiency also affects overall growth
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets in children, characterised by soft, poorly mineralised bones; because Vitamin D can be synthesised in skin exposed to sunlight, limited outdoor time compounds the risk when dietary sources such as fish and egg yolk are also lacking.
questions.hint: Recall which vitamin's synthesis pathway specifically depends on sunlight exposure on the skin.
distractor_logic: Vitamin K's well-established deficiency symptom is increased blood-clotting time, not soft bones, and it is not described as being synthesised via sunlight exposure.
Vitamin E deficiency is linked to increased fragility of red blood cells and muscular weakness, not to soft, poorly mineralised bones.
Vitamin B1 deficiency is specifically linked to beriberi, a nerve-related condition, not to soft or poorly mineralised bones.

questions.question: A sample of nucleic acid is analysed and found to contain uracil but no thymine, along with a sugar that has a free -OH group at the 2' position. This sample is most likely:
options: A carbohydrate polymer with no nitrogen-containing components
DNA, since DNA is the more commonly discussed nucleic acid
A protein, since it contains nitrogen-bearing bases
RNA, since it contains ribose (with a 2'-OH) and uracil in place of thymine
questions.explanation: The presence of uracil, rather than thymine, and a sugar retaining a 2'-hydroxyl group, ribose rather than 2'-deoxyribose, are both diagnostic of RNA rather than DNA.
questions.hint: Match both the base (uracil versus thymine) and the sugar (2'-OH present or absent) to the correct nucleic acid.
distractor_logic: The sample explicitly contains uracil, a nitrogenous base, so it cannot be a carbohydrate polymer lacking nitrogen.
The presence of uracil and a sugar with a free 2'-OH, ribose rather than deoxyribose, specifically points away from DNA, which contains thymine and 2'-deoxyribose.
Nitrogenous bases, sugars, and phosphate groups are components of nucleic acids, not proteins, which are built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

questions.question: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds. Based on this pattern, a DNA sample with a higher percentage of G-C base pairs relative to A-T base pairs would be expected to:
options: Require more energy, such as a higher temperature, to separate its two strands, because of the greater number of hydrogen bonds per G-C pair
Contain more thymine than adenine overall
Have fewer total hydrogen bonds overall than a sample with more A-T pairs, regardless of composition
Have single-stranded rather than double-stranded regions exclusively
questions.explanation: Since G-C base pairs are held together by three hydrogen bonds compared to the two hydrogen bonds of A-T pairs, DNA regions or samples richer in G-C content require more thermal or chemical energy to separate the two strands.
questions.hint: Compare the number of hydrogen bonds per base pair for G-C versus A-T, and think about what more hydrogen bonds implies for strand separation.
distractor_logic: Within a double helix, adenine and thymine are always present in equal amounts due to their obligate pairing; differing G-C content does not by itself create an imbalance between A and T.
Each individual G-C pair has more, three, hydrogen bonds than each A-T pair, two, so a higher proportion of G-C pairs tends to increase total hydrogen bonding for a similarly sized DNA molecule.
The base-pairing pattern described is characteristic of double-stranded, base-paired DNA regions, not single-stranded DNA, which lacks this systematic pairing.

questions.question: The two strands of the DNA double helix are described as 'antiparallel'. What does this specifically mean?
options: One strand contains only purines and the other contains only pyrimidines
The two strands run in opposite 5' to 3' directions relative to each other
The two strands are made of completely different types of sugar
The two strands never come into contact with each other
questions.explanation: In the DNA double helix, the two polynucleotide strands run in opposite directions, one 5' to 3' and the complementary strand 3' to 5', which is what is meant by describing them as antiparallel.
questions.hint: Focus on the directionality of each strand's sugar-phosphate backbone, from its 5' end to its 3' end.
distractor_logic: Each strand of DNA contains a mixture of purine and pyrimidine bases; antiparallel refers to backbone directionality, not a segregation of base types by strand.
Both strands of DNA use the same sugar, deoxyribose; 'antiparallel' refers to the directionality of the sugar-phosphate backbones, not a difference in sugar type.
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonding between paired bases across the helix, so they are in close contact; antiparallel describes their relative orientation, not their separation.

questions.question: A biochemist isolates a nucleotide and determines it contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups linked in series. This molecule is best identified as a component related to:
options: A standard DNA building block, since adenine is one of DNA's bases
A fatty acid used in lipid storage
ATP (adenosine triphosphate), an energy-carrying nucleotide derivative
An amino acid used in protein synthesis
questions.explanation: A nucleotide built from adenine, ribose, and three linked phosphate groups corresponds to ATP, a specialised nucleotide that functions as the cell's primary energy-carrying molecule rather than as a routine structural unit of a nucleic acid strand.
questions.hint: Note the unusual detail, three phosphate groups rather than the single phosphate found in a typical nucleic-acid-strand nucleotide.
distractor_logic: The presence of ribose, rather than deoxyribose, and three phosphate groups, rather than the single phosphate typical of a routine nucleic-acid-chain nucleotide, point away from a standard DNA building block.
The components described, a nitrogenous base, a sugar, and phosphate groups, are characteristic of a nucleotide, not a fatty acid, which is a long hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxyl group.
Amino acids are characterised by amino and carboxyl functional groups on a carbon skeleton, not by a nitrogenous base, sugar, and multiple phosphate groups.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: If a segment of one DNA strand reads 5'-A-T-G-C-3', what would the base sequence of the complementary strand be, following strict Watson-Crick pairing and the antiparallel convention?
options: 3'-T-A-C-G-5', equivalent to 5'-G-C-A-T-3'
A strand of entirely unrelated, randomly chosen bases
5'-A-T-G-C-3', identical to the original strand
5'-U-A-C-G-3', using uracil in place of thymine
questions.explanation: Applying strict Watson-Crick base pairing to the given strand and reversing the direction for the antiparallel complementary strand gives 3'-T-A-C-G-5', equivalent to 5'-G-C-A-T-3'.
questions.hint: Pair each base with its Watson-Crick partner, then remember the two strands run in opposite directions.
distractor_logic: Base pairing in DNA is governed by strict complementarity rules, A with T and G with C, not by random assignment.
Complementary strands are not identical in sequence; each base pairs with its specific partner, so the new strand's sequence must differ accordingly.
The complementary strand of DNA is still DNA and uses thymine, not uracil; uracil replaces thymine specifically in RNA.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: During protein synthesis, a change (mutation) in the DNA base sequence can sometimes lead to a structurally different, non-functional protein being made. What does this illustrate about the relationship between DNA and proteins?
options: DNA and proteins are entirely unrelated biomolecules with no functional connection
The DNA base sequence, via transcription and translation, ultimately determines the amino acid sequence of a protein
Mutations always improve the function of the resulting protein
Proteins determine the base sequence of DNA, not the other way around
questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the central role of DNA as the carrier of genetic information: its base sequence, transcribed into mRNA and translated at the ribosome, specifies the amino acid sequence of a protein, so a change in that base sequence can alter or abolish the protein's normal structure and function.
questions.hint: Trace the direction of information flow described in the chapter, from DNA base sequence to the final protein.
distractor_logic: This directly contradicts the phenomenon described, in which a DNA-level change alters the protein produced.
The scenario describes a mutation leading to a non-functional protein, illustrating that mutations often disrupt rather than improve function.
This reverses the actual direction of information flow, in which DNA sequence directs the amino acid sequence of the protein via mRNA.

questions.topic: Nucleic Acids – Replication, Genetic Code & Functions
questions.question: During translation, a ribosome reads the mRNA sequence and tRNA molecules deliver amino acids in a corresponding order. If a small segment of mRNA is altered so that it now specifies a different amino acid at one position, what is the most likely downstream consequence?
options: The DNA itself would automatically be altered to match the new mRNA sequence
No change at all, since mRNA sequence has no bearing on the protein made
A protein with a different amino acid at that one position in its primary structure, which could alter its folding and function
The ribosome would stop functioning permanently for all future protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Since the mRNA sequence specifies which amino acid tRNA delivers at each position during translation, altering that sequence at one point changes the corresponding position in the resulting protein's amino acid sequence, potentially affecting its structure and biological activity.
questions.hint: Focus on how mRNA sequence and amino acid incorporation are directly linked during translation.
distractor_logic: Information flow in this process runs from DNA to mRNA to protein; a change introduced at the mRNA level does not, by itself, rewrite the original DNA template.
This contradicts the fundamental process of translation, in which mRNA sequence directly specifies which amino acids are incorporated into the protein.
An altered mRNA affects only the protein being translated from that particular message; it does not permanently disable the ribosome's general capacity to translate other mRNA molecules.

questions.question: Insulin (a peptide hormone) and testosterone (a steroid hormone) both act as chemical messengers, but they are built from very different types of molecules. Which contrast correctly reflects this difference in their chemical nature?
options: Insulin is a steroid, and testosterone is a peptide
Both insulin and testosterone are built from long carbohydrate chains
Both are amino-acid derivatives, differing only in which single amino acid they are made from
Insulin is built from a chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, while testosterone is derived from a cholesterol-based steroid skeleton
questions.explanation: Insulin is a peptide hormone built from chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, while testosterone belongs to the structurally distinct class of steroid hormones derived from cholesterol.
questions.hint: Recall the three broad chemical classes hormones are grouped into, and which class each of these two examples belongs to.
distractor_logic: This reverses their actual classifications; insulin is the peptide hormone, and testosterone is the steroid hormone.
Neither hormone is a carbohydrate; insulin is a protein and testosterone is a steroid.

Amino-acid-derivative hormones like adrenaline are built from a single modified amino acid, whereas insulin is a full polypeptide of many linked amino acids, and testosterone is steroid-derived, not amino-acid-derived.

questions.question: Thyroxine, an amino-acid-derivative hormone containing iodine, regulates the body's basal metabolic rate. If thyroxine production falls significantly below normal, which broad category of physiological effect would most directly follow, based on its described function?
options: An immediate and permanent loss of the primary structure of all proteins in the body
An increase in blood clotting time, similar to Vitamin K deficiency
A general slowing of metabolic processes, consistent with thyroxine's role in regulating metabolic rate
A complete failure of DNA replication in all cells
questions.explanation: Since thyroxine functions to regulate the body's metabolic rate, a significant deficiency in its production would be expected to slow metabolic processes generally, consistent with its described physiological role.
questions.hint: Focus specifically on the one physiological function attributed to thyroxine in the chapter.
distractor_logic: Thyroxine deficiency is described as a metabolic-regulation issue, not a direct cause of protein primary-structure breakdown throughout the body.
Increased blood-clotting time is specifically associated with Vitamin K deficiency, not with reduced thyroxine levels, which relate to metabolic rate.
Thyroxine's described role concerns regulation of metabolic rate, not direct control over the DNA replication process.

questions.question: Oxytocin and vasopressin are both hormones associated with the pituitary gland and are chemically classified as peptide hormones, like insulin. What does this chemical classification imply about how they are built?
options: They are built entirely from glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds
They are composed of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds, similar in bonding type to proteins generally
They contain no nitrogen atoms at all
They are built from a steroid nucleus derived from cholesterol, like testosterone
questions.explanation: Because oxytocin and vasopressin are classified as peptide hormones, they are built from amino acids linked through peptide bonds, the same type of bond that links amino acids in proteins generally.
questions.hint: Recall what 'peptide' implies about the type of bond and building blocks used to construct these hormones.
distractor_logic: Glycosidic-linked glucose units describe carbohydrates such as starch or glycogen, not peptide hormones, which are built from amino acids.
As peptide hormones built from amino acids, oxytocin and vasopressin necessarily contain nitrogen in their amide and amino/side-chain groups.
A steroid-based structure describes hormones such as testosterone and estrogen, not peptide hormones such as oxytocin, vasopressin, and insulin.

questions.question: A carbohydrate X does not reduce Tollens' reagent in its native form. Complete acid hydrolysis of X yields only glucose, and the amount of glucose obtained (by mass, after accounting for the water taken up in hydrolysis) corresponds to hundreds of repeating glucose units per molecule of X. Which class of carbohydrate is X, and what specifically distinguishes it from a disaccharide that also yields only glucose?
options: X is a disaccharide, since maltose also yields only glucose on hydrolysis
X cannot be identified from this data because carbohydrates cannot be classified by hydrolysis products
X is a monosaccharide, since it ultimately breaks down to glucose

X is a polysaccharide; unlike a glucose-only disaccharide such as maltose, X yields hundreds of glucose units rather than exactly two, and its lack of reducing character reflects the negligible proportion of free anomeric ends in such a large molecule
questions.explanation: Yielding hundreds of glucose units on hydrolysis identifies X as a polysaccharide (such as starch or glycogen); its lack of reducing character in the intact form arises because, in a molecule of that size, only a vanishingly small fraction of units carry a free anomeric end, unlike a disaccharide such as maltose, which is a small molecule with one readily detectable free anomeric -OH.
questions.hint: Compare both the number of units released on hydrolysis and what fraction of a very large molecule could realistically carry a free reducing end.
distractor_logic: A disaccharide such as maltose yields exactly two glucose units on hydrolysis and is itself reducing; X yields hundreds of units and is non-reducing, both inconsistent with maltose.

Classification of carbohydrates by the number of monosaccharide units obtained on hydrolysis is precisely the standard basis used to distinguish monosaccharides, oligosaccharides, and polysaccharides.
A monosaccharide cannot be hydrolysed into simpler units at all; X clearly undergoes hydrolysis to release many glucose units, ruling out a monosaccharide.

questions.question: Compound P is non-reducing and hydrolyses to give two different monosaccharides in a 1:1 ratio. Compound Q is reducing and also hydrolyses to give two different monosaccharides in a 1:1 ratio. Both P and Q are disaccharides of glucose with a second sugar. What is the essential structural difference between P and Q that accounts for their different reducing behaviour, given both release the same total number and ratio of units?
options: P must be a polysaccharide in disguise, since non-reducing sugars are always polysaccharides
In P, the glycosidic bond involves both anomeric carbons of the two component sugars, whereas in Q, only one anomeric carbon is involved, leaving one free anomeric -OH
P and Q must differ in molecular formula, with P containing fewer oxygen atoms than Q
Q must contain a different type of glycosidic bond that is easily hydrolysed by water alone at room temperature, while P's bond is not hydrolysable at all
questions.explanation: The key structural distinction between a reducing disaccharide like maltose or lactose and a non-reducing one like sucrose is whether one or both anomeric carbons are consumed in forming the glycosidic bond; using both anomeric carbons (as in P, matching sucrose's pattern) removes any free carbonyl-generating centre, while using only one (as in Q) leaves a free anomeric -OH capable of opening to a reactive carbonyl.
questions.hint: Think about what specifically differs between sucrose-type and maltose-or-lactose-type glycosidic linkages, independent of which particular monosaccharides are involved.
distractor_logic: Non-reducing character is not exclusive to polysaccharides; sucrose is a classic non-reducing disaccharide, demonstrating that disaccharides can also be non-reducing depending on which carbons form the glycosidic bond.

P and Q, both being disaccharides formed by loss of one water molecule between two hexose units, would have essentially the same general molecular formula pattern; the reducing-behaviour difference is structural (which carbons form the glycosidic bond), not a difference in overall atom count.

Both P and Q are described as hydrolysing to give their component monosaccharides; both are therefore hydrolysable, and reducing character is unrelated to ease of hydrolysis under these described conditions.

questions.question:
The Haworth structures below represent two anomers of D-glucopyranose, differing only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon.

Based on standard D-glucopyranose convention (where the -CH2OH at C5 points upward), which structure represents β-D-glucopyranose, and why?
options: Structure Y, because its C1 -OH group points upward, on the same side as the C5 -CH<sub>2</sub>OH group, which is the defining orientation for the β-anomer
Structure X, because its C1 -OH group points downward, which is the defining orientation for the β-anomer
Neither structure can be β-D-glucopyranose, since β-D-glucopyranose does not exist as a stable ring form
Both X and Y represent β-D-glucopyranose, since anomers are identical in all respects
questions.explanation: By convention, in a Haworth projection of a D-hexopyranose with the ring oxygen at the back-right and the C5 -CH<sub>2</sub>OH group drawn upward, the β-anomer has its anomeric (C1) -OH group also pointing upward (on the same side as C5's substituent), while the α-anomer has it pointing downward; this matches structure Y.
questions.hint: Compare the orientation of the C1 -OH group to the orientation of the C5 -CH<sub>2</sub>OH group in each structure.
distractor_logic: A C1 -OH pointing downward, opposite to the C5 -CH<sub>2</sub>OH group, is the defining orientation for the α-anomer, not the β-anomer.
β-D-glucopyranose is a well-characterised, stable cyclic hemiacetal form of glucose, and in fact predominates over the α-form at mutarotation equilibrium.
Anomers are, by definition, not identical; they differ specifically in the configuration at the anomeric carbon, which is exactly what distinguishes structures X and Y here.

questions.question: A chemist treats D-glucose with excess methanol under acidic conditions, converting the anomeric -OH into a -OCH<sub>3</sub> group to form methyl D-glucoside, while leaving all other -OH groups unreacted. Predict how methyl D-glucoside would behave in a Fehling's test and a mutarotation experiment, compared to free D-glucose.
options: Methyl D-glucoside would give a strongly positive Fehling's test because methanol itself is a reducing agent

Methyl D-glucoside would give a negative Fehling's test and would not show mutarotation, because the anomeric carbon is now permanently locked as a methyl acetal, unable to reopen to the free aldehyde form
Methyl D-glucoside would behave identically to free glucose in both tests, since methylation of a single -OH does not affect the rest of the molecule
Methyl D-glucoside would show even faster mutarotation than free glucose, since methylation increases the molecule's reactivity
questions.explanation: Once the anomeric -OH is converted into an acetal (as in methyl D-glucoside), the ring can no longer open back to the free aldehyde form, so the molecule permanently retains one fixed anomeric configuration; without a way to regenerate a free carbonyl, it can neither reduce Fehling's solution nor undergo mutarotation, both of which specifically require a free (or freely re-exposable) anomeric centre.
questions.hint: Both mutarotation and the Fehling's test outcome depend on the same structural feature: whether the anomeric carbon can reopen to a free carbonyl group.
distractor_logic: Fehling's test detects a free or freely generated aldehyde group on the sugar; methanol's own chemical reactivity is irrelevant here, and the methylated anomeric carbon can no longer open to expose an aldehyde group.

The specific -OH that is methylated here is the anomeric one, which is uniquely responsible for both the ring-opening equilibrium (mutarotation) and the reducing behaviour; converting it into a fixed acetal removes both properties, unlike methylation of a non-anomeric -OH.

Mutarotation depends on the ring being able to open back to the free carbonyl form; locking the anomeric carbon as a methyl acetal prevents this ring-opening entirely, so mutarotation is abolished, not accelerated.

questions.question: A hexose is treated with excess phenylhydrazine and gives an osazone identical to glucosazone, but the hexose itself does not give a positive Schiff's test (a test that specifically requires a free aldehyde, unmasked by any adjacent functional group interference) as readily as glucose does, despite reducing Fehling's solution. This hexose is most consistent with being:
options: Galactose, since it also forms glucosazone and behaves identically to glucose in the Schiff's test
Sucrose, since sucrose also reduces Fehling's solution
A second molecule of glucose, since only glucose is known to form glucosazone

Fructose, since it forms the same osazone as glucose (both being altered only at C1 and C2 during osazone formation) but, as a ketose, does not react with Schiff's reagent in the same direct way an aldehyde does
questions.explanation: Since osazone formation only involves the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon, glucose and fructose give an identical osazone despite being an aldose and a ketose respectively; fructose's ketonic (rather than aldehydic) carbonyl explains why its behaviour with a strictly aldehyde-selective test like Schiff's reagent differs from glucose's, even though both reduce Fehling's or Tollens' reagent through enolisation pathways.
questions.hint: Recall which sugar, despite matching glucose's osazone, has a fundamentally different type of carbonyl group that a strictly aldehyde-specific test could distinguish.
distractor_logic: Galactose, an aldohexose differing from glucose in configuration at a carbon beyond C2, forms a different osazone from glucose, and, being an aldose, would be expected to respond to Schiff's reagent in the same manner as glucose, unlike the hexose described here.
Sucrose is a disaccharide, not a hexose, and, critically, does not reduce Fehling's solution at all because both its anomeric carbons are tied up in its glycosidic bond.

Fructose independently forms the identical glucosazone, since osazone formation only modifies C1 and C2, which is precisely why glucose and fructose cannot be distinguished by this specific test alone.

questions.question: In a mixture containing equal moles of D-glucose and D-fructose, the observed specific rotation is measured and found to be laevorotatory overall, even though D-glucose alone is dextrorotatory. If instead the mixture contained three moles of D-glucose for every one mole of D-fructose, predict, using approximate specific rotation values (glucose about +52°, fructose about −92°), what the net optical rotation of this new mixture would most likely be.
options: The mixture's rotation cannot be predicted or estimated from the specific rotations of its components
Exactly zero rotation, since the mixture would now be perfectly optically inactive
Net dextrorotatory, because the much larger relative amount of glucose would now outweigh fructose's stronger but now minority contribution
Still net laevorotatory, with exactly the same magnitude as the equimolar mixture
questions.explanation: Weighting each sugar's specific rotation by its relative molar proportion, three parts glucose (roughly 3 × +52° = +156, in weighted terms) versus one part fructose (roughly 1 × −92° = −92) gives a net positive (dextrorotatory) result, in contrast to the equimolar mixture, where fructose's larger magnitude dominates and produces a net laevorotatory result.
questions.hint: Weight each sugar's specific rotation by its relative proportion in the mixture rather than simply comparing the two specific rotation values directly.
distractor_logic: For an ideal mixture of two optically active compounds that do not interact, the net observed rotation can reasonably be estimated as the mole-weighted sum of each component's specific rotation contribution.

A 3:1 glucose-to-fructose ratio, using the given specific rotation magnitudes, gives glucose's combined positive contribution (about 3 × 52 = 156) clearly outweighing fructose's negative contribution (about 1 × 92 = 92); this does not sum to zero.

Changing the molar ratio from 1:1 to 3:1 in glucose's favour changes the weighted contribution of each sugar to the net rotation; the outcome should not remain numerically identical to the equimolar case.

questions.question: Sucrose is hydrolysed by the enzyme invertase to give invert sugar. Suppose a chemist instead partially hydrolyses a sucrose solution and stops the reaction before completion, then tests the resulting mixture with Fehling's solution. The mixture gives a positive test. What does this observation imply about the mixture's composition, and why would fully unreacted sucrose alone not give this result?
options: The positive test indicates a laboratory error, since partially hydrolysed sucrose should behave identically to fully intact sucrose
Fehling's solution reacts with the glycosidic bond of sucrose directly, regardless of whether hydrolysis has occurred

The mixture contains some free glucose and fructose released by partial hydrolysis, and these monosaccharides, unlike intact sucrose, have free anomeric -OH groups capable of reducing Fehling's solution
Sucrose itself must be a reducing sugar after all, contradicting everything established about its structure
questions.explanation: As sucrose is partially hydrolysed, some glucose and fructose are released; unlike intact sucrose, these free monosaccharides each retain an anomeric carbon capable of opening to a reactive carbonyl form, so even a partially hydrolysed mixture will test positive with Fehling's solution, unlike fully intact sucrose alone.
questions.hint: Consider what new, smaller molecules are generated as hydrolysis proceeds, and how their anomeric carbons differ from those in the original disaccharide.
distractor_logic: Partial hydrolysis, by definition, converts some sucrose into its monosaccharide components, which are reducing sugars; this predictably changes the mixture's behaviour compared to fully intact sucrose.

Fehling's solution specifically detects a free or freely accessible carbonyl group; it does not react with an intact glycosidic linkage, which is precisely why unhydrolysed sucrose gives a negative test.

Sucrose's non-reducing character, arising from both anomeric carbons being engaged in its glycosidic bond, is a well-established structural fact; the positive test here is explained by hydrolysis products being present, not by sucrose itself suddenly becoming reducing.

questions.question: A researcher has three unlabelled white powders, each a pure disaccharide: one is maltose, one is sucrose, and one is lactose. Using only Fehling's test and acid hydrolysis followed by testing the hydrolysate for the presence of a ketohexose (a specific test that only fructose, and no other product from these three disaccharides, would give a positive result for), design a logical identification scheme and determine which single powder can be identified directly, without hydrolysis, using only the Fehling's test.
options: Maltose can be identified directly, since it is the only one that yields a ketohexose on hydrolysis

None of the three can be identified by Fehling's test alone, since maltose and lactose both give a positive Fehling's test; hydrolysis and the ketohexose test are needed to distinguish sucrose (negative Fehling's, positive ketohexose test after hydrolysis) from the other two, and a further step is needed to distinguish maltose from lactose
All three can be distinguished by Fehling's test alone, without any need for hydrolysis
Sucrose can be identified directly, since it is the only one of the three that gives a positive Fehling's test
questions.explanation: Fehling's test alone separates sucrose (negative, non-reducing) from maltose and lactose (both positive, reducing), but cannot by itself distinguish maltose from lactose, since both are reducing disaccharides; a further step, such as identifying the hydrolysis products (glucose and galactose for lactose versus only glucose for maltose), is needed to complete the identification.
questions.hint: First determine which single test result can cleanly separate one disaccharide from the other two, then consider what further information is needed to separate the remaining pair.
distractor_logic: Maltose hydrolyses to give only glucose, an aldohexose; it is sucrose, not maltose, that yields a ketohexose (fructose) on hydrolysis.
Fehling's test alone only distinguishes sucrose (negative) from the other two (both positive); maltose and lactose cannot be told apart by Fehling's test alone, since both are reducing sugars.

Sucrose is precisely the one disaccharide among these three that gives a negative Fehling's test, since both of its anomeric carbons are engaged in its glycosidic bond; maltose and lactose both give positive Fehling's tests.

questions.question: If cellulose (a β-1,4-linked glucose polymer) could somehow be converted, without changing molecular formula, into a compound with the same α-1,4 linkage pattern found in amylose, what direct functional consequence would this have for human digestion, and why?
options: The converted polymer would become toxic to humans, since altering glycosidic linkages generally produces harmful compounds
The converted polymer would no longer be classified as a carbohydrate
The converted polymer would become digestible by human amylase, since human digestive enzymes are specific for the α-1,4-glycosidic linkage found in starch, unlike the β-1,4 linkage of cellulose
There would be no change in digestibility, since digestibility depends only on molecular formula, not on the stereochemistry of the glycosidic linkage
questions.explanation: Human amylase and related digestive enzymes are specific for the α-1,4-glycosidic linkage characteristic of starch; since cellulose's indigestibility in humans stems specifically from its β-1,4 linkages (which human enzymes cannot hydrolyse), converting those linkages to the α form found in amylose would, in principle, make the resulting polymer digestible.
questions.hint: Recall precisely why cellulose resists digestion by human enzymes in the first place, and what change would remove that specific obstacle.
distractor_logic: Changing the stereochemistry of a glycosidic linkage from β to α does not inherently create a toxic compound; in this case, it would simply convert an indigestible polysaccharide into a digestible one, analogous to starch.
A polymer of glucose units joined by glycosidic linkages remains a carbohydrate regardless of whether the linkage is α or β; only its digestibility and some physical properties would change.

Human digestive enzymes such as amylase are specific to the stereochemical configuration of the glycosidic bond, not merely to the overall molecular formula; changing β-1,4 to α-1,4 linkages, while keeping the same formula, would change which enzymes can act on the polymer.

questions.question: A branched glucose polysaccharide sample is analysed and found to contain, per 1000 glucose residues, roughly 40 α-1,6-glycosidic branch points. A second, related sample from a different biological source contains only about 20 α-1,6 branch points per 1000 residues under the same analysis. Based on the chapter's description of starch and glycogen, which sample is more likely to be glycogen, and why?
options: Neither sample can be glycogen, since glycogen contains no α-1,6 linkages at all
The sample with about 20 branch points per 1000 residues, since glycogen is described as completely unbranched
Both samples are equally likely to be glycogen, since branch-point frequency has no bearing on distinguishing starch components from glycogen
The sample with about 40 branch points per 1000 residues, since glycogen is described as more highly branched than amylopectin, the branched component of starch
questions.explanation: Since glycogen is described as structurally similar to amylopectin but with even more frequent branching, the sample with the higher density of α-1,6 branch points (about 40 per 1000 residues) is more consistent with glycogen, while the more sparsely branched sample better fits amylopectin.
questions.hint: Recall the specific comparative claim made about glycogen's branching frequency relative to amylopectin's.
distractor_logic: Glycogen, like amylopectin, contains α-1,6 linkages specifically at its branch points, in addition to the α-1,4 linkages along its chains; the presence of α-1,6 branch points is consistent with, not contrary to, glycogen's structure.
Glycogen is not unbranched; it is described as even more highly branched than amylopectin, making the more sparsely branched sample less consistent with glycogen.

The chapter specifically distinguishes glycogen from amylopectin partly on the basis of glycogen's greater branching frequency, so a higher branch-point count is a meaningful clue rather than an irrelevant detail.

questions.question: A sample of processed starch is treated exhaustively with a debranching enzyme that specifically cleaves α-1,6-glycosidic bonds without affecting α-1,4 bonds. After this treatment, the resulting product is analysed and found to consist entirely of long, unbranched glucose chains. What can be concluded about the original starch sample's amylopectin component, and what does the resulting product structurally resemble?
options: The amylopectin's branch points were selectively removed, leaving behind only its originally unbranched α-1,4-linked segments, so the product structurally resembles amylose
The treatment must have destroyed all the glucose units, since removing branch points should eliminate the entire polysaccharide
No meaningful conclusion can be drawn, since debranching enzymes are not relevant to understanding polysaccharide structure
The product must now be cellulose, since cellulose is also an unbranched glucose polymer
questions.explanation: Because the debranching enzyme removes only the α-1,6 branch-point linkages while leaving α-1,4 linkages intact, the resulting long, unbranched chains represent what was originally the unbranched, α-1,4-linked backbone segments of amylopectin, structurally resembling amylose, which is itself an unbranched α-1,4-linked glucose polymer.
questions.hint: Track exactly which bond type is cleaved and which is preserved, and consider what kind of structure remains once only one bond type is removed.
distractor_logic: Cleaving only the α-1,6 branch-point bonds leaves the α-1,4-linked backbone segments intact; the glucose units and their α-1,4 linkages remain, simply now as separate unbranched chains rather than one interconnected branched molecule.

Selectively removing branch points while leaving straight-chain linkages intact is a chemically meaningful way to probe how much of a branched polysaccharide's mass exists as unbranched segments, directly informing its structure.

Cellulose is unbranched but consists of β-1,4-linked glucose units; the debranching enzyme in this scenario only cleaves α-1,6 bonds and does not alter the α-configuration of the remaining α-1,4 linkages, so the product retains the α-linkage pattern of amylose, not the β-linkage pattern of cellulose.

questions.question: A dipeptide is formed from two different amino acids, X and Y, each of which individually has an isoelectric point close to neutral pH. If X's carboxyl group condenses with Y's amino group to form the peptide bond, which functional groups remain free (uncombined) at the two ends of the resulting dipeptide, and what does this imply about the dipeptide's own acid-base behaviour?
options: Both the amino and carboxyl groups of both X and Y are consumed in forming the peptide bond, leaving the dipeptide with no ionisable groups at all
The dipeptide retains two free amino groups and no free carboxyl groups

X's free amino group remains at one end and Y's free carboxyl group remains at the other end, so the dipeptide, like a single amino acid, can still act as an amphoteric species with its own characteristic ionisable groups
The dipeptide has no defined ends, since peptide bond formation makes the molecule fully cyclic
questions.explanation: In forming the peptide bond, X's -COOH reacts with Y's -NH<sub>2</sub>, consuming exactly one carboxyl and one amino group; X's own -NH<sub>2</sub> and Y's own -COOH remain unreacted at the two ends of the dipeptide, so, like a single amino acid, the dipeptide retains ionisable amino and carboxyl termini and can behave amphoterically.
questions.hint: Track exactly which specific functional group from each amino acid is consumed in forming the new peptide bond, and which groups from each amino acid are left untouched.
distractor_logic: Peptide bond formation consumes only one carboxyl group (from X) and one amino group (from Y); X's amino group and Y's carboxyl group are not involved in this particular bond and remain free.

Since only X's carboxyl group reacted with Y's amino group, the amino group that remains free belongs to X (at one end), while the carboxyl group that remains free belongs to Y (at the other end); the dipeptide does not end up with two free amino groups and no carboxyl groups.
Peptide bond formation between two amino acids, as described here, produces a linear dipeptide with a free amino end and a free carboxyl end, not a cyclic structure.

questions.question: Two amino acids, one with a side chain (R group) bearing an extra -COOH and one with a side chain bearing an extra -NH<sub>2</sub>, are mixed in solution at physiological pH (around 7). Based on their classification as acidic and basic amino acids respectively, predict the direction each would migrate in an electrophoresis experiment (an experiment that separates charged species based on their net charge, by movement toward oppositely charged electrodes) at this pH, relative to a neutral amino acid run alongside them.
options: The acidic amino acid, carrying a net negative charge from its extra ionised carboxyl group, would migrate toward the positive electrode, while the basic amino acid, carrying a net positive charge from its extra protonated amino group, would migrate toward the negative electrode
Both amino acids would remain stationary, exactly like the neutral amino acid, since all amino acids have the same net charge at physiological pH
Migration direction cannot be predicted from acidic or basic classification alone
The acidic amino acid would migrate toward the negative electrode, and the basic amino acid would migrate toward the positive electrode
questions.explanation: At physiological pH, an acidic amino acid's extra carboxyl group is predominantly ionised to -COO<sup>−</sup>, giving it a net negative charge and causing migration toward the positive electrode (anode), while a basic amino acid's extra amino group is predominantly protonated to -NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, giving it a net positive charge and causing migration toward the negative electrode (cathode); a neutral amino acid at its isoelectric point shows no net migration.
questions.hint: Work out the net charge each amino acid would carry at physiological pH based on its acidic or basic classification, then recall that opposite charges migrate toward opposite electrodes.
distractor_logic: Acidic and basic amino acids, by definition, carry a net negative or net positive charge respectively at physiological pH due to their extra ionisable side-chain group, unlike a neutral amino acid, which carries no net charge at its isoelectric point; they would not remain stationary like the neutral amino acid.

The acidic/basic classification of an amino acid is specifically based on its net charge tendency at physiological pH arising from an excess of carboxyl or amino groups, which directly predicts its electrophoretic migration direction.

This reverses the expected direction: a species with a net negative charge migrates toward the positive electrode, and a species with a net positive charge migrates toward the negative electrode; the acidic amino acid (net negative) should move toward the positive electrode, not the negative one.

questions.question:
The schematic below shows the condensation of two amino acids to form a dipeptide.

Based on this schematic, if a tripeptide were formed by adding one more amino acid to the dipeptide shown (condensing a third amino acid's -NH2 group with the dipeptide's free -COOH terminus), how many peptide bonds and how many water molecules would have been eliminated in total across the whole tripeptide-forming process?
options: Three peptide bonds and three water molecules, since there are three amino acids involved in total
One peptide bond and one water molecule in total, since only one condensation reaction is shown in the schematic
No water molecules are eliminated in polypeptide formation, only in polysaccharide formation
Two peptide bonds and two water molecules in total: one of each for the original dipeptide-forming step shown, and one more of each for adding the third amino acid
questions.explanation: Joining three amino acids into a tripeptide requires two condensation (peptide-bond-forming) steps in total, the one shown in the schematic plus one more to add the third amino acid, and each step eliminates one water molecule, giving two peptide bonds and two water molecules overall.
questions.hint: Count the number of connections needed to link three amino acids in a chain, not simply the number of amino acids.
distractor_logic: The number of peptide bonds formed corresponds to the number of condensation reactions (connections between consecutive amino acids), which is always one fewer than the number of amino acids joined; three amino acids joined in a chain form two peptide bonds, not three.

The schematic shows only the first condensation (forming the dipeptide); the question asks about the total across both steps, the one shown plus the additional step of adding a third amino acid, which together involve two separate condensation reactions.

Peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction, just like glycosidic bond formation, and does eliminate a water molecule for each bond formed, as shown explicitly in the schematic's −H<sub>2</sub>O label.

questions.question: A protein is subjected to a treatment that selectively breaks disulfide bonds and hydrogen bonds but leaves all peptide (covalent backbone) bonds completely intact. After this treatment, the protein loses its biological activity and its original compact shape. Based on this outcome, at which structural level(s) has this treatment acted, and what has it specifically left unchanged?
options: The treatment has disrupted secondary, tertiary, and possibly quaternary structure (all of which depend on hydrogen bonds and, for tertiary/quaternary structure, disulfide bonds), while leaving the primary structure, the amino acid sequence itself, completely unchanged
The treatment has altered the primary structure, since the protein's activity has changed
The treatment has converted the protein into a carbohydrate, since its shape has changed
The treatment has had no real structural effect, since the peptide bonds are unaffected
questions.explanation: Since hydrogen bonds stabilise secondary structure (and contribute to tertiary and quaternary structure) and disulfide bonds stabilise tertiary and quaternary structure, breaking both while leaving peptide bonds intact denatures the protein by disrupting its higher-order folding, while its primary structure, the covalently linked amino acid sequence, remains unaffected.
questions.hint: Match each type of bond mentioned, hydrogen and disulfide versus peptide, to the specific level(s) of protein structure it is responsible for maintaining.
distractor_logic: The scenario explicitly states that peptide bonds, which define the amino acid sequence (primary structure), remain intact; loss of activity here results from disrupted higher-order structure, not from any change to the sequence itself.

A change in shape due to loss of hydrogen and disulfide bonds is a denaturation event affecting protein conformation; it does not convert the protein into an entirely different class of biomolecule such as a carbohydrate.

Even though peptide bonds are unaffected, disrupting hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds removes the interactions that maintain a protein's secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, which is precisely why the protein loses its shape and activity.

questions.question: A globular protein is dissolved in water at physiological pH and temperature, where it is biologically active. The solution is then made strongly acidic and heated briefly, after which it is neutralised and cooled back to physiological conditions. The protein does not regain its original activity. Contrast this outcome with what would be expected if only the pH (not the temperature) had been changed and then reversed, and explain the difference in terms of the severity of denaturation.
options: Neither scenario involves true denaturation, since the protein is returned to physiological pH and temperature at the end in both cases
Denaturation by heat and acid combined should always be more easily reversible than denaturation by pH change alone
There should be no difference at all between the two scenarios, since both involve denaturation of the same protein

Combined strong-acid and heat treatment often causes more extensive, effectively irreversible unfolding and aggregation of the protein's tertiary structure, whereas a milder, purely pH-based change is sometimes reversible if the original folded state can be recovered once neutral pH is restored
questions.explanation: Denaturation severity depends on the extremity and combination of the conditions applied; a brief, strong combined assault (high temperature plus strong acid) is more likely to cause extensive, often irreversible unfolding and aggregation than a milder, single-variable change such as pH alone, which some proteins can recover from once the original conditions are restored.
questions.hint: Think about how the combination and intensity of denaturing conditions, not just their eventual reversal, affects whether a protein can refold correctly.
distractor_logic: Returning to the original conditions afterward does not by itself guarantee that the protein refolds correctly; denaturation refers to the loss of native structure during the treatment, and this loss may or may not be reversed afterward, which is exactly the distinction the question is asking about.

This is the reverse of what is generally expected; combining multiple denaturing stresses, such as heat and strong acid, tends to make unfolding more severe and less likely to be reversible than a single, milder stress such as pH change alone.

Denaturation is not a strictly all-or-nothing phenomenon; its reversibility can depend on the severity and combination of denaturing conditions, so a combined heat-and-acid treatment is not necessarily equivalent in outcome to a milder, purely pH-based change.

questions.question: An enzyme's rate of product formation is measured at increasing substrate concentrations while enzyme concentration is held constant. Initially, the rate increases roughly in proportion to substrate concentration, but at high substrate concentrations, the rate levels off and further increases in substrate concentration produce little additional increase in rate. Using the lock-and-key model of enzyme action, explain why this levelling-off (saturation) occurs.
options: At high substrate concentrations, the substrate itself stops being chemically reactive

At high substrate concentrations, essentially all of the fixed number of enzyme active sites are continuously occupied, so adding more substrate cannot further increase the rate at which enzyme-substrate complexes can form and turn over
At high substrate concentrations, the enzyme is permanently destroyed by excess substrate, explaining the levelling off
The levelling-off indicates that enzymes do not actually follow the lock-and-key model at high substrate concentrations
questions.explanation: Since each enzyme molecule has a fixed number of active sites (typically one), at high substrate concentrations these sites become continuously occupied and are working at their maximum turnover capacity; adding still more substrate cannot increase the rate further because there are no additional free active sites available to bind it, producing the observed saturation.
questions.hint: Consider what physically limits how many enzyme-substrate complexes can form at any one moment, given a fixed amount of enzyme.
distractor_logic: The substrate's inherent chemical reactivity does not change with its concentration; the levelling-off in rate is explained by the enzyme's limited number of active sites becoming saturated, not by any change in the substrate itself.

The lock-and-key model describes a reversible, non-destructive interaction between enzyme and substrate; saturation of rate is explained by the enzyme's active sites becoming fully occupied, not by enzyme destruction.

Saturation kinetics at high substrate concentration is, in fact, a predicted and well-explained consequence of the lock-and-key model once one considers that the enzyme has a fixed, limited number of active sites available at any given enzyme concentration.

questions.question: A vitamin-derived molecule is found to bind tightly to a specific site on an enzyme, distinct from where the substrate normally binds, and this binding is required for the enzyme to catalyse its reaction at a normal rate. If this vitamin-derived molecule is entirely absent from the diet for a prolonged period, predict the most likely effect on the enzyme's catalytic activity and connect this to why certain vitamin deficiencies can produce widespread metabolic symptoms.
options: The enzyme would instead start acting on a completely different substrate in the absence of the vitamin-derived molecule
The substrate itself would be destroyed in the absence of the vitamin-derived molecule, even without any enzyme present
The enzyme's activity would be unaffected, since vitamins only affect digestion, not other enzyme-catalysed reactions

The enzyme's catalytic activity would be substantially reduced or lost despite the enzyme protein itself being structurally present, because it lacks the vitamin-derived cofactor needed for normal function, which helps explain why some vitamin deficiencies disrupt many metabolic reactions at once
questions.explanation: Many enzymes require small non-protein helper molecules (cofactors or coenzymes), some of which are derived from vitamins, to achieve their catalytically active conformation or to participate directly in the reaction mechanism; without the vitamin-derived cofactor, the enzyme protein may be structurally present but catalytically impaired, which is part of why deficiencies of certain vitamins can disrupt multiple metabolic pathways that depend on such enzymes.
questions.hint: Distinguish between the enzyme protein itself being present and the enzyme being able to function without a required helper molecule.
